## About This User Guide

This user guide describes PXL, the IC Validator architecture, command-line options, and other basic information.

This user guide is designed to enhance both beginning and advanced users' knowledge of PXL, the IC Validator architecture, and command-line options.

This preface includes the following sections:

- New in This Release
- Related Products, Publications, and Trademarks
- Conventions
- Customer Support
- Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity

## New in This Release

Information about new features, enhancements, and changes, known limitations, and resolved Synopsys Technical Action Requests (STARs) is available in the IC Validator Release Notes on the SolvNetPlus site.

## Related Products, Publications, and Trademarks

[https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com](https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com/)

## Conventions

The following conventions are used in Synopsys documentation.

| Convention     | Description                                                                                                                                                           |
|----------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Courier        | Indicates syntax, such as write_file                                                                                                                                  |
| Courier italic | Indicates a user-defined value in syntax, such as write_file design_list                                                                                              |
| Courier bold   | Indicates user input-text you type verbatim-in examples, such as prompt> write_file top                                                                               |
| Purple         | • Within an example, indicates information of special interest. • Within a command-syntax section, indicates a default, such as include_enclosing = true &#124; false |
| [ ]            | Denotes optional arguments in syntax, such as write_file [-format fmt ]                                                                                               |
| ...            | Indicates that arguments can be repeated as many times as needed, such as pin1 pin2 ... pinN .                                                                        |
| &#124;         | Indicates a choice among alternatives, such as low &#124; medium &#124; high                                                                                          |
| \              | Indicates a continuation of a command line.                                                                                                                           |
| /              | Indicates levels of directory structure.                                                                                                                              |
| Bold           | Indicates a graphical user interface (GUI) element that has an action associated with it.                                                                             |
| Edit > Copy    | Indicates a path to a menu command, such as opening the Edit menu and choosing Copy .                                                                                 |
| Ctrl+C         | Indicates a keyboard combination, such as holding down the Ctrl key and pressing C.                                                                                   |

Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee, customer, and partner feels welcomed. ## IC Validator Basics

This chapter gives a brief overview of the IC Validator physical verification tool. It also describes the IC Validator command-line options and distributed processing.

The basics of the IC Validator tool are described in the following sections:

- Using the IC Validator Tool in Your Design Flow
- IC Validator Command-Line Options
- Compiler Directives
- Exit Codes
- Inlined Functions
- Distributed Processing
- Runset Caching
- Using IC Validator Command-Line Options With Runset Caching
- Layer Mapping
- Using PXL Runset Encryption

## Using the IC Validator Tool in Your Design Flow

All IC Validator runs are executed based on your IC Validator runset. You can execute the IC Validator tool using command-line execution, interactive execution using VUE, or from various other Synopsys tools, such as the StarRC or IC Compiler tools. To load IC Validator, you must set two environment variables:

- Set ICV\_HOME\_DIR to the IC Validator installation directory
- Set PATH to include $ICV\_HOME\_DIR/bin

<!-- image -->

To run the IC Validator tool successfully in your design flow,

- Create and debug a runset file. The runset file includes the following information:
- Layout database specifics
- General options
- Layer assignments
- Database checks, such as snap and grid checks
- Design rule checking (DRC), electrical rule checking (ERC), fill patterns, or layoutversus-schematic (LVS) checking
- Run IC Validator DRC and ERC on your layout database, verifying your design against the design rule document.
- Review and debug errors generated in the IC Validator DRC and ERC run using IC Validator error files or VUE.
- Run the IC Validator tool to perform fill-pattern generation, including basic DRC checks on the layers that are filled.
- Run IC Validator LVS checking.
- Review and debug errors generated in the IC Validator LVS run using IC Validator error files or VUE.

See Appendix A, IC Validator Architecture.

## Running the IC Validator Tool Within the IC Compiler Tool

You can run the IC Validator tool from inside the IC Compiler tool; this flow is called InDesign physical verification. For this flow, use the following IC Compiler commands:

- signoff\_drc signof \_drc, IC mple a . Performs DRC checking using a foundry-qualified IC Validator DRC runset.
- signoff\_autofix\_drc signof \_metal , IC p r c d . Performs automatic DRC repair. In this flow, the IC Validator tool.
- Performs signoff DRC checking.
- Generates route guidance that assists the router in performing targeted repairs.
- Validates the repair done by the router.
- signoff\_metal\_fill signof \_metal , IC p r c d . Inserts metal and via fill in either pattern-based mode, which uses a foundry-qualified IC Validator metal-fill runset, or in track-based mode, which

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

uses information from the technology file. The fill shapes are written into a FILL view of the Milkyway design.

- signoff\_fix\_isolated\_via . Performs automatic fixing of isolated vias.
- report\_metal\_density . Calculates the metal density and density gradient values and annotates the values on the design.

## Note:

You must make sure that the IC Validator tool can parse and run the runset before using it within the IC Compiler tool.

See the IC Compiler Implementation User Guide , which is available on SolvNetPlus, or the IC Compiler man pages for detailed command syntax and usage.

## Running the IC Validator Tool Within the IC Compiler II Tool

You can run the IC Validator tool from inside the IC Compiler II tool; this flow is called InDesign physical verification. For this flow, use the following IC Compiler II commands:

- signoff\_check\_drc signof \_che k dr , IC mpl a . Performs DRC checking using a foundry-qualified IC Validator DRC runset.
- signoff\_fix\_drc signof \_ x drc, IC mple a . Performs automatic DRC repair. In this flow, the IC Validator tool
- Performs signoff DRC checking.
- Generates route guidance that assists the router in performing targeted repairs.
- Validates the repair done by the router.
- signoff\_create\_metal\_fill signof \_creat m l , IC p d . Inserts metal and via fill in either pattern-based mode, which uses a foundry-qualified IC Validator metal-fill runset, or in track-based mode, which uses information from the technology file. The fill shapes are written into the design view of the IC Compiler II input design.
- signoff\_fix\_isolated\_via . Performs automatic fixing of isolated vias.

## Note:

You must make sure that the IC Validator tool can parse and run the runset before using it within the IC Compiler II tool.

See the IC Compiler II Implementation User Guide , which is available on SolvNetPlus, or the IC Compiler II man pages for detailed command syntax and usage.

<!-- image -->

## Running the IC Validator Tool With StarRC Parasitic Extraction

You can generate IC Validator data for input to the StarRC tool, using the following functions as part of the IC Validator runset:

- The functions for parasitic extraction (PEX) layer mapping are
- pex\_conducting\_layer\_map() ◦ pex\_via\_layer\_map() ◦ pex\_marker\_layer\_map() ◦ pex\_remove\_layer\_map() ◦ pex\_viewonly\_layer\_map() ◦ pex\_ignore\_cap\_layer\_map()

These functions map IC Validator polygon\_layer objects to StarRC TCAD\_GRD\_FILE layers to generate a layer mapping file for use with the StarRC tool.

- The function for generating a connected layout database and mapping files for input to StarRC parasitic extraction is
- pex\_generate\_results()

Table 1 shows the LVS settings that are not supported for use in the IC Validator-StarRC flow. These settings should be set to false .

Table 1

LVS Settings Not Supported for IC Validator-StarRC Flow

| Unsupported setting                | Argument default   | Recommended setting   |
|------------------------------------|--------------------|-----------------------|
| compare(memory_array_compare=true) | true               | false                 |
| merge_series(multiple_paths=true)  | false              | false                 |

See the IC Validator Reference Manual for detailed syntax and usage of the parasitic extraction functions.

## Running the IC Validator Tool From the Custom Compiler Platform

You can run the IC Validator tool for DRC and LVS from the Custom Compiler platform using its Verification menu or from the Custom Compiler command line. See the Custom Compiler documentation, which is available on SolvNetPlus, for more information.

## Setting Up and Running DRC

You can set up and run DRC from the Custom Compiler platform using its Verification menu:

1. In your Layout window, choose Verification &gt; DRC &gt; Setup and Run.
2. Select the IC Validator tool and specify all the required runtime parameters.
3. Click Apply or OK to run the IC Validator tool.

## Note:

To view the output, select the View Output check box to open the Custom Compiler Text Viewer. Using tabs in the viewer, you can see the runset, results, errors, and a log of the run.

To run the IC Validator tool with parameters previously set in the Setup and Run menu, choose Verification &gt; DRC &gt; Run.

You can start an IC Validator VUE debugging session from the Custom Compiler platform.

- After an IC Validator run, to run VUE from the Custom Compiler platform, choose Verification &gt; DRC &gt; Debug.
- To run VUE when the Setup menu has not been set to ICV,
- Set the preference db::setPrefValue xtDRCTool -value icv .
- Choose Verification &gt; DRC &gt; Debug.

To open the Custom Compiler Text Viewer, which provides access to the runset, cell .RESULTS, cell .LAYOUT\_ERRORS, and the stdout.drc.log files, choose Verification &gt; DRC &gt; View Output.

## Setting Up and Running LVS

You can set up and run LVS from the Custom Compiler platform using its Verification menu:

1. In your Layout or Schematic window, choose Verification &gt; LVS &gt; Setup and Run.
2. Select the IC Validator tool and specify all the required runtime parameters.
3. Click Apply or OK to run the IC Validator tool.

## Note:

To view the output, select the View Output check box to open the Custom Compiler Text Viewer. Using tabs in the viewer, you can see the runset, results, errors, and a log of the run.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

To run the IC Validator tool with parameters previously set in the Setup and Run menu, choose Verification &gt; LVS &gt; Run.

You can start an IC Validator VUE debugging session from the Custom Compiler platform.

- After an IC Validator run, to run VUE from the Custom Compiler platform, choose Verification &gt; LVS &gt; Debug.
- To run VUE when the Setup menu has not been set to ICV,
- Set the preference db::setPrefValue xtLVSTool -value icv .
- Choose Verification &gt; LVS &gt; Debug.

To open the Custom Compiler Text Viewer, which provides access to the runset, cell .RESULTS, cell .LAYOUT\_ERRORS, cell .LVS\_ERRORS, and the stdout.lvs.log files, choose Verification &gt; LVS &gt; View Output.

## IC Validator Command-Line Options

The IC Validator command-line syntax is as follows:

```
icv [ command-line-options ] [ runsetfile ]
```

where runsetfile is a set of instructions written in PXL, which tells IC Validator how to perform the required checking operations. In most cases, a runset file is required. There are some exceptions, for example, when comparing two netlists, or when adding or removing hosts to a run.

This section of the manual describes the command-line options that can be used with IC Validator. They are organized into categories based on their purpose as follows:

- Common
- Host Configuration
- Runset Configuration
- DRC
- LVS / PERC
- Explorer
- Input Database
- Output
- Debug

- Optimization Controls
- Licensing
- General

## Common

Table 2 IC Validator Common Command-Line Options

| Option                                      | Definition                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|---------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Common                                      | Options used often in most flows.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| runsetfile                                  | IC Validator runset.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| -c cell -c om and li e pt , v r g w h       | Overrides the cell argument cel nam , o d- i pt in the library() function and the layout_top_cell argument in the compare() function. By specifying -cell "*" you can run the IC Validator tool using the OASIS or GDSII format without specifying the top cell. The IC Validator tool finds the top cell in the database. If there is more than one potential top cell, the IC Validator tool chooses the first one it finds in the database and prints a warning message in the summary file. Do not use -cell "*" in these situations: • LVS runsets, that is, runsets with a call to the compare() function. • Runsets that call the get_top_cell() function before the end of the ASSIGN section. • Along with the -ndg or -C command-line options. • Runsets that set the select_window or exclude_window argument of the incremental_options() function. • Databases that are not in GDSII or OASIS format. |
| -f format -f com and li e pt br y , v g w h | Overrides the library format libra y fo m t, c nd- e p (GDSII, Milkyway, NDM, OASIS, or OpenAccess) specified in the library() function.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| -vue -vue com and li pt                     | Creates VUE output VUEcom and-li e pt . Creating VUE output can also be enabled by setting the create_vue_output argument in the error_options() function to true .                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

## Host Configuration

| Option             | Definition                                                  |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| Host Configuration | Options to specify the hosts, CPUs, memory, and disk usage. |

Table 3 IC Validator Host Configuration Command-Line Options

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Table 3 IC Validator Host Configuration Command-Line Options (Continued)

| Option                                                                                                                | Definition                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| -host_init hostname &#124; number_of_cpus &#124; hostname:number_of_cpus &#124; LSF &#124; SGE &#124; NB &#124; SLURM | Starts an IC Validator job on a single host or multiple hosts. See Specifying Host Names and CPU Counts for more information. Examples: • -host_init hostname . Runs on the given host and uses all of the CPUs. • -host_init number_of_cpus . Runs on the local host and uses the specified number of CPUs. • -host_init hostname:number_of_cpus . Runs on the given host and uses the specified number of CPUs. • -host_init LSF . Automatically determines host and number of CPUs from Platform LSF environment. • -host_init SGE . Automatically determines host and number of CPUs from the Univa Grid Engine environment • -host_init NB . Automatically determines host and number of CPUs from the NetBatch environment. • -host_init SLURM . Automatically determines host and number of CPUs from the SLURM environment. Note: Use the sbatch batch submission command to submit jobs and not the srun command which is not suitable for multihost submissions. Note: When using the hostname and number_of_cpus syntax, the argument to the -host_init command-line option can be specified multiple times, for example, -host_init hosta:8 hostb:8 |
| -host_disk                                                                                                            | Specifies a local group directory for all hosts specified with -host_init or -host_add . Examples: • icv -host_init hostA:32 -host_disk /SCRATCH/user/group_1 • icv -host_add hostB:32 -host_disk /SCRATCH/user/group_1 Note: If the local disk space becomes 100 percent full while the tool is running, the tool no longer uses the local directory path, but instead uses only the network path of the run_details directory. By default, the write_vue_info function does not use the directory specified by the -host_disk command-line option. To override this behavior, set the _ICV_NI_USE_HOST_DISK environment variable. Use this option when the -host_disk directory provides significantly better performance than the run directory.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

Table 3 IC Validator Host Configuration Command-Line Options (Continued)

## Option

-host\_login

-host\_memory Memory\_Value M|G|T

-host\_add hostname | number\_of\_cpus | hostname:number\_of\_cpus | LSF | SGE | NB | SLURM

-host\_remove list\_of\_hosts

-host\_thread\_mode SMT | &lt;value&gt;

## Definition

Enables the IC Validator tool to log in to remote hosts to start processes for a distributed job. Ensure that the tool locates the binary/script supplied to -host\_login . The default is rsh .

- icv -host\_login ssh

## Examples:

- icv -host\_login "qrsh -inherit"

Your specification of -host\_login always takes precedence over other settings including overridding the login mechanism used for -host\_init/-host\_add LSF|SGE|NB|SLURM .

## Note:

Attempts to maintain the user-specified target memory for the hosts used in the IC Validator job by rescheduling and threading. This switch cannot be used to reduce the memory of a single command.

- -host\_memory 1000M

-host\_memory 10T

-host\_memory 100G

The maximum value of this command-line option is the actual physical memory of the machine.

## Note:

The -host\_init and -host\_add command-line options support the -host\_memory command-line option. Unless the -host\_memory command-line option is specified on the command line, the IC Validator tool never sets any memory targets. The -host\_add command-line option does not inherit any memory settings from the main job.

Adds more hosts (including remote hosts) to an IC Validator job that is already running. The usage is the same as the usage for -host\_init . See Specifying Host Names and CPU Counts for more information.

## Note:

By default, -host\_add only supports single host grid requests. Use multiple host\_add submissions to add more than one host.

Removes the list of hosts from the IC Validator job.

All IC Validator processes and commands linked to the running job are shut down for the listed hosts (if this host was acquired through a host reservation system, the host can be released).

- -host\_thread\_mode SMT . Uses simultaneous multithreading (SMT) enabled CPUs for threading.
- -host\_thread\_mode &lt;value&gt; . Dedicates a percentage of CPUs to be used for threading. The value must be between 0 and 100.

## Note:

SMT is evaluated before &lt;value&gt; when both options of -host\_thread\_mode are provided.

There are three categories of selection rules: select or suppress by violation comment ( -svc and -uvc ), by violation name ( -svn and -uvn ), and by function ( -sfn and -ufn ). The arguments |
| -uvc     | violation_comment                                         | name                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| -svn     | violation_name -svn com a d li e pt -uvn com a d li e pt  | • Can include the wildcard * and range expressions using [ ].                                                                                                                                                                                            |

|          | function -ufn com a d li e pt                             | on a command line. For example,                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

- For each category, selection is based on what is selected and not suppressed. Final selection is the intersection of the violations selected in each category.
- % icv -svc "*96A1*" -svc "*11B16*"
- If the selection option is not used for a category but the suppression option is used, then all violations excluding those suppressed are selected for that category.
- If the final selection of violations is empty, the run terminates with an error.
- If both selection and suppression options are missing for a category, then for that category all violations are selected. If you do not use any of the options, the whole runset is selected.

The -svc and -uvc , -svn and -uvn , and -sfn and -ufn specifications (along with any runset-based violation\_name\_[un]select() or violation\_comment\_select() specifications), construct a matched list of rules by comment, name, and function, respectively. By default, these three lists are intersected to produce the finalized "selected" violation list. Using the -smu command-line option, this list is joined by union to produce the finalized "selected" violation list.

| -bct option -bct | Blocks forward data flow analysis through the outputs of specified commands. The selections for option are: • extent . The extent functions whose output is blocked are cell_extent() , cell_extent_layer() , layer_extent() , and chip_extent() . • connect . The connect functions whose output is blocked are connect() , incremental_connect() , stamp() , and stamp_edge() . • both . The output of both extent and connect functions is blocked. • none . Forward data flow analysis is not blocked. This value is the default. The -bct command-line option must be used with the -il or -iln command-line options. You can use all three options together. The selection of the specified commands, however, is not blocked. For example, if there is a data flow path from an incremental assign layer to a check that requires output from a connect() function, the connect() functions are not blocked even if the -il layer_name -bct connect command-line options are used. |

-il " layer ... layer "

Defines the incremental layers to be used in an incremental-by-layer run by layer name.

- Specify multiple names with spaces as separators.
- Put the set of layer names within quotation marks.

For example,

```
-il "POLY" -il "POLY DIFF METAL"
```

## Note:

When the name argument of an assign function is not used, the layer name for the assign is from the left side assignment, for example,

Layer names specified in the name argument of any assign function are used for matching incremental assign layer names.

layer\_name = assign(...) .

If more than one layer name is specified, incremental processing occurs if one or more layer names are found in the ASSIGN section. Layer names that are not found are ignored. If none of the specified layers are found in the ASSIGN section, the IC Validator tool exits with an error message.

The violations that are based, directly or indirectly, on the incremental layers are executed in the IC Validator run. The other violations are not executed in the IC Validator run.

In general, IC Validator OPTIONS and ASSIGN section functions fall into this category. See Inlined Functions for a complete list of the runset functions that are tagged with the inline qualifier. ## Compiler Directives

## Support for 64-Bit Coordinates

The IC Validator tool converts coordinate data to a signed 32-bit integer coordinate space. Large die sizes with a small database resolution might require a larger integer space, causing a coordinate overflow error to occur.

To increase the coordinate space, use the -64 command-line option. Only use the -64 option when it is required; this is because the memory usage increases.

The value limits for a 32-bit integer are:

- Maximum positive value: 2,147,483,647

- •

- Maximum negative value: -2,147,483,648

In the following example,

- Rcoord is a real number xy coordinate value.
- I coord is the coordinate converted to an integer.

<!-- image -->

## Assume the following values:

- Rcoord   = 25,000.1234 mm (2.50001234 cm from 0.0000)
- Working resolution = 2x

For a database resolution of 0.0001 mm, the Rcoord value does not overflow the 32-bit integer coordinate space:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

For a database resolution of 0.00001, the Rcoord value overflows the 32-bit integer coordinate space:

I coord = 25,000.1234*(1/0.00001)*2 = 5,000,024,680 &gt; 2,147,483,647

Not all overflows, however, are created equally. Before using the -64 option, make sure that you are using all of the available coordinate space. As shown in Figure 1, using only positive coordinate values artificially limits the maximum die size.

Figure 1 Overflow of the 32-Bit Integer Coordinate Space

<!-- image -->

Center the die about the origin to maximize available coordinate space, as shown in Figure 2. Using the -64 option is not needed to prevent an overflow.

<!-- image -->

Figure 2 No Overflow of the 32-Bit Integer Coordinate Space

<!-- image -->

The IC Validator error database is enhanced with a variable-width coordinate format that can accommodate either 32-bit or 64-bit integer coordinates. This applies to both the error databases (PYDB) and the error classification databases (cPYDB), which might be exported for DRC error classification.

The pydb\_export utility is enhanced with the ability to convert error classification databases (cPYDB) among the various coordinate formats to maintain compatibility as necessary.

## Note:

Current and future IC Validator tools retain support for reading error databases with the older fixed 32-bit or 64-bit coordinate formats. However, IC Validator tools prior to version L-2016.06 are not able to read the new coordinate format.

## Run-Only Execution

Follow these steps for run-only execution.

1. Identify the sections of the runset for which you want the required runset checks with these directives:

```
#pragma runonly begin #pragma runonly end
```

You can define multiple run-only sections within a runset.

<!-- image -->

2. Call the IC Validator tool with -ro , the run-only command-line option, to
- a. Parse the runset.
- b. Prune the runset functions that do not have data flow into run-only code sections.
- c. Execute the pruned runset.

## Note:

If the IC Validator tool does not find a run-only section within a runset, the runset is not executed.

3. Alternatively, to stop execution after the runset is parsed and pruned for run-only execution, use the -pcr command-line option along with -ro . For example,
4. Use the -nro command-line option when using pruned run-only output as the source runset. If you do not use the -nro option, default pruning optimizations can eliminate functions inside run-only code sections.

```
% icv -ro -pcr outfile
```

## Note:

All #pragma run-only directives remain in the pruned run-only output.

The presence of #pragma run-only directives in the pruned run-only output enables the icv -ro runonly.rs command line to be used for execution of the output pruned runonly.rs runset.

## Environment Variables

The $ sign preceding a variable indicates the variable is an environment variable. For example,

```
$ENV_ABC
```

The variable must be set in the environment; otherwise a parse error occurs. All environment variables are considered strings. For example,

```
if( $ENV_ABC == "XYZ") { x = abc(XYZ); } else { x = abc(NOT_XYZ) }
```

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Providing Additional Information to the Compiler

#pragm env [ ]co il d t s b , The compiler directive #pragma envvar interfaces with environment variables to

- Print a list containing the names and the values of each specified environment variable.

```
#pragma envvar report variable ... variable
```

If any variable does not exist, an error occurs. For example,

```
error: #pragma envvar references undefined environment variable 'e'
```

- Probe the environment for the named variable.
- If the named variable exists, no action is taken.
- If the named variable does not exist, the value of the variable in the environment is set to the concatenation of the rest of the line. The concatenation must be a sequence of string literals or references to other environment variables, or both.

```
// input file #pragma envvar default x "aa" #pragma envvar default y "bb" #pragma envvar default z $x "__" $y // Use $X notation to // reference defined // variables #pragma envvar report x y z // output from compiler a.rs:4: x=aa a.rs:4: y=bb a.rs:4: z=aa__bb
```

#pragma envvar default variable ... variable

## Note:

If there is more than one #pragma envvar default statement that defines the same variable, subsequent occurrences see the variable as already set in the environment, as set by the first occurrence.

## Creating Preprocessor Definitions From Environment Variables

#pragm env [ ]co il d t s b , The preprocessor #pragma PXL define\_from\_envvar creates a preprocessor definition from an environment variable, if the environment variable is set. The syntax is

```
#pragma PXL define_from_envvar cpp_var env_var
```

The preprocessor definition named by cpp\_var is given the value of the environment variable named by env\_var , as if by a #define command. If the environment variable is not set, no action is taken, such that cpp\_var remains undefined or retains its previous definition.

<!-- image -->

The preprocessor #pragma PXL define\_from\_envvar takes two arguments:

- The first argument is the name of the preprocessor definition to redefine if the environment variable is set.
- The second argument is the name of the environment variable to get the value from.

```
#include <icv.rh> #define str(x) #x #define qstr(x) str(x) #if defined(FOO_DEF) note("Before pragma, defined as: " + qstr(FOO_DEF)); #else note("Not defined before pragma"); #endif #pragma PXL define_from_envvar FOO_DEF FOO_ENV #if defined(FOO_DEF) note("After pragma, defined as: " + qstr(FOO_DEF)); #if FOO_DEF == 2 note("... and satisfies test for == 2"); #elif FOO_DEF == 3 note("... and satisfies test for == 3"); #endif #else note("Not defined after pragma"); #endif When the run is as follows: % export FOO_ENV=3 % icv -verbose -D FOO_DEF=2 define_from_envvar.rs The output is: define_from_envvar.rs:10: Before pragma, defined as: 2 define_from_envvar.rs:17: After pragma, defined as: 3 define_from_envvar.rs:21: ... and satisfies test for == 3
```

Notice the original value is 2 because of the preprocessor definition that passed on the command line. The define\_from\_envvar pragma redefines FOO\_DEF to a value of 3 . If FOO\_ENV is not set, FOO\_DEF is has a value of 2 . If FOO\_DEF is also not defined on the command line, it remains undefined for the remainder of the preprocessing.

<!-- image -->

Use the #if definition( identifier , string , case\_sensitivity ) function in conjunction with the define\_from\_envvar pragma to support the querying of the $envvar\_name environment variable to determine if it has a value of string .

In the user environment, set this:

```
setenv BEOL_STACK 9M_3Mx_2Fx_2Dx_1Gx_1Iz_LB
```

## The runset looks like this:

```
#pragma PXL define_from_envvar d_ENV_BEOL_STACK BEOL_STACK #if definition(d_ENV_BEOL_STACK, "9M_3Mx_2Fx_2Dx_1Gx_1Iz_LB", 0) ... #endif #if definition(d_ENV_BEOL_STACK, "8M_2Mx_2Fx_2Dx_1Gx_1Iz_LB", 0) ... #endif
```

- The third argument, #case\_sensitivity , is used on define\_identifiers (definition( identifier , string , case\_sensitivity ) , and is explicitly #defined in the runset, without the need for envvar . With a value of 0 , this argument performs a case-insensitive comparison between the identifier's value and the specified string. With a value of 1 , this argument performs a case-sensitive comparison.

## Pruning Layers

The #pragma prune\_assign compiler directive tells the IC Validator tool to read-only the required runset layers from input design and create the required runset layers. You can use this compiler directive to enable or to disable pruning:

```
#pragma icv compiler [enable|disable] prune_assign
```

When this compiler directive is not used or is disable and the -prune\_assign commandline option is not used, the IC Validator tool reads all of the runset layers from the input design. In all cases, unnecessary runset layers are not reported in the summary file. The setting of the prune\_assign directive in the runset has priority over the -prune\_assign command-line option.

## Prioritizing the Scheduling of Functions

The #pragma prioritize directive increases the scheduling priority for the function and the functions it depends on. Place the #pragma prioritize directive immediately before the targeted command or code block. This directive might also assign extra threads to those prioritized functions. For example,

<!-- image -->

```
#pragma prioritize not_rectangles(M5); The #pragma prioritize directive increases the priority for both of the not_rectangles() functions, as shown in the following example: #pragma prioritize ERR_M4 @= { @ "M4 non-rectangles"; not_rectangles(M4); not_rectangles(M5); }
```

See Table 15 for related command-line options.

The functions in the -runset\_config file are processed in accordance with the following criteria:

- All of the OPTIONS functions are effectively inserted into the runset after the last option.
- All of the 'compare setup' functions are inserted just after the last 'compare setup' function.
- Any options specified in compare() itself are used to update compare in the runset.

## Runset Insertion

Runset insertion allows you to customize the main runset using secondary runsets without the need for modifying the main runset. If the main runset includes the necessary pragma statements to indicate where code can be inserted, you can provide additional runset code in a separate file.

The syntax in the main runset is #pragma icv insert &lt;label&gt; . This pragma can only be used one time per &lt;label&gt; . All of these pragmas must be on their own line.

After the insertion pragma is specified, you can mark a block of code by setting #pragma icv label &lt;label&gt; begin and #pragma icv label &lt;label&gt; end . These pragmas must come after the corresponding insert pragma. They cannot be nested or overlap. Multiple blocks of code using the same &lt;label&gt; are allowed and are inserted into the same destination in the order they are defined.

<!-- image -->

|                    | Inputs                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |                              | ndno                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| foundry_runset.rs  | #include <icv.rh> #pragmaicvinsertoptions M1 = assign({{1}}); V1 =assign(({(2}}); M2 = assign(({3}}): #pragma icv insert assigns V1_M1 @= {V1 not M1; } V1_M2 @= {V1 not M2:} #pragma icv insert checks final_checks(); | internal runset to be parsed | #include<icv.rh> M1 = assign({{1}): V1 = assign({{2}}); M2 = assign(({(3}}); boundary = assign(({255}}): V1_M1 @={V1 not M1; } V1_M2@={V1 not M2:} CHECK _BOUNDARY @= not_inside(M1,boundary); not_inside(M2,boundary): |
| user_patch_file.rs | #pragma icv label assigns begin boundary = assign(({255}}); #pragma icv label assigns end #pragma icvlabel checksbegin CHECK_BOUNDARY @= not_inside(M1,boundary); not_inside(M2,boundary); #pragma icv label checks end | internal runset to be parsed | final_checks();                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

## Inlined Functions

When you run the IC Validator tool with the -ndg command-line option,

- Any user function that invokes an inline runset function needs to be tagged with the inline qualifier. See Table 17 for a list of inline runset functions. For example,
- User functions that call runset functions with cell lists and call runset functions used to construct cell lists also must be tagged with the inline qualifier. See Table 18 for a list of functions. For example,

```
my_options : inline function ( void ) returning void { . . . error_options(...); gds_options(...); . . . }
```

```
add_strings_to_list : inline function (string_list : in_out list of string, new_strings : list of string) returning void { string_list = string_list.merge(new_strings); } get_cell_extent : inline function (layer1 : polygon_layer, cells : list of string) returning result : polygon_layer { result = cell_extent(layer1, cells); } cells : list of string = {}; add_strings_to_list(cells, {"AX", "AY", "AZ"}); add_strings_to_list(cells, {"BX", "BZ"}); part_extent = get_cell_extent(part, cells);
```

If a user function needs to be tagged with the inline qualifier but it does not have the qualifier, the runtime error is:

```
error: unable to extract cell list for no explode options
```

## Distributed Processing

You can run the IC Validator tool in a variety of different distributed processing situations, including using multiple CPUs on a single host and using multiple hosts.

Running the IC Validator tool with distributed processing provides the following features:

- Scalability increases with the number of CPUs used
- Flexibility for adding CPUs to an existing IC Validator job
- Simultaneous multithreading

Distributed processing is described in the following sections:

- Specifying Host Names and CPU Counts
- License Requirements

## Specifying Host Names and CPU Counts

The IC Validator tool takes advantage of multiple CPUs on a host by determining automatically whether to start parallel tasks or multithread. You must communicate to the tool how many CPUs on the host you want to use. You can do this by using the -host\_init command-line option.

For example, to use 8 CPUs on a single host, use the following command-line option:

```
icv -host_init 8 runset.rs
```

It is possible to specify which host to run on. In the preceding example, the host name was omitted, so the local host was assumed. If you specify a different host name, the IC Validator tool starts on that host. In the following example, 8 CPUs are used on hostA.

```
icv -host_init hostA:8 runset.rs
```

Because a remote host is specified, the IC Validator tool must make a connection to that host. By default, the tool attempts to use the rsh command to make this connection. If a different connection method is needed, use the -host\_login command-line option (some IT environments might disable rsh access or require a different connection method). In the following example, 8 CPUs are used on hostA and ssh is used to connect to the host.

<!-- image -->

```
icv -host_init hostA:8 -host_login /bin/ssh runset.rs
```

## Note:

IC Validator uses rsh as the host login program by default when available. Using rsh can be considered a security risk and is frequently discouraged and disabled. If rsh is disabled in your environment, IC Validator automatically uses ssh . Disabling rsh at the system level is the recommended way to enforce the security policy for all users on your network. You can also set the -host\_login command-line option to always use ssh when launching IC Validator (for example, -host\_login ssh ).

You can list more than one host. In this case, the IC Validator tool uses all of the hosts listed, with the number of CPUs specified. In the following example a total of 32 CPUs are used: 8 CPUs on the local host; 8 on hostA; and 16 CPUs on hostB (because the -host\_login command-line option is NOT specified, rsh connects to the hosts).

```
icv -host_init 8 hostA:8 hostB:16 runset.rs
```

You can enable additional threads on the hosts that support simultaneous multithreading (SMT). In the following example, on a host with two logical CPUs per core, the IC Validator tool dedicates 8 CPUs for commands and 8 additional CPUs for threading.

```
icv -host_init 8 -host_thread_mode SMT
```

See the -host\_init and -host\_login command-line options in IC Validator CommandLine Options for more information.

## Note:

If the host name is specified but the CPU count is omitted, ALL of the CPUs are used on the host.

After the job is running, you can add more CPUs. Hosts and CPUs are specified in the same way using the -host\_add command-line option. Notice that this job must be run from the same working directory as the original IC Validator job. If the run\_details directory was specified in the initial run using -rd , this directory must also be specified on this run using -rd .

## Modifying Resources for a Running Job

You can add more CPUs to a running IC Validator job. Hosts and CPUs are specified with the -host\_add command-line option, in the same way that they are specified with the -host\_init command-line option.

The following example adds 16 CPUs on hostC to the running job.

```
icv -host_add hostC:16
```

## Note:

When using -host\_add , most of the other command-line options are unnecessary and not allowed. See -host\_add in Table 3 for more information.

You can also remove hosts from a running job. Hosts are specified using the -host\_remove command-line option. It is only possible to remove entire hosts. The following example removes all of hostC (all of its CPUs) from the running job.

```
icv -host_remove hostC
```

You can instruct IC Validator to automatically add and remove hosts from the running job. Hosts are added when too many commands are queued and are removed when the hosts are idle. This can be specified when the job is originally started or after the job is running. You must provide the command that IC Validator should use to acquire a new host. The command must include an icv -host\_add on the acquired host.

For the -host\_init , -host\_add , and -host\_elastic command-line options, this IC Validator call must be run in the same working directory as the running job. Furthermore, if the run\_details directory was specified in the initial running run using -rd , this directory must also be specified on this run using -rd . All command-line options are ignored with the following exceptions: -rd is used by all three of these options, and -host\_login / -host\_disk is used by -host\_add .

## Running in LSF

When running in LSF, the syntax and preceding examples are still appropriate. The following example shows how to launch an LSF job that starts IC Validator on 16 CPUs on a single host, using the bsub command.

```
bsub -n 16 -R "span[ptile=16]" <bsub options> icv -host_init 16 runset.rs
```

Similarly, to add 16 CPUs on one host to a running IC Validator job, use the -host\_add command-line option. For example,

```
bsub -n 16 -R "span[ptile=16]" <bsub options> icv -host_add 16
```

As a convenience, the IC Validator tool can automatically determine the host configuration and sets -host\_login to blaunch . To enable this feature, specify LSF as the as the argument to -host\_init . In the following example, 16 CPUs are requested on a single host using bsub and are identified using the LSF argument of the -host\_init commandline option.

```
bsub -n 16 -R "span[ptile=16]" <bsub options> icv -host_init LSF runset.rs
```

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

This feature is most useful when requesting jobs on multiple hosts. The following example works with multiple hosts as well (2 hosts, 16 CPUs each):

```
bsub -n 32 -R "span[ptile=16]" <bsub options> icv -host_init LSF runset.rs
```

The LSF argument also works with the -host\_add command-line option. In this example, a total of 64 CPUs are added to a running job: 8 hosts each with 8 CPUs.

```
bsub -n 64 -R "span[ptile=8]" <bsub options> icv -host_add LSF
```

To elastically add hosts to the job, specify a bsub command to the host\_elastic command-line option that acquires a machine and starts the IC Validator tool. In the following example, a single host is requested with 8 CPUs. (Depending on your environment, you might need to provide additional arguments to bsub.)

```
bsub -n 8 'span[hosts=1]' icv -host_add LSF
```

Add this entire string to the host\_elastic command-line option or specify in a separate script. The complete IC Validator command can look as follows:

```
icv -host_init 16 -host_elastic "bsub -n 8 'span[hosts=1]' icv -host_add LSF" runset.rs
```

## Running in Univa Grid Engine (UGE/SGE)

When running in SGE, the syntax and preceding examples are still appropriate. The following example shows how to launch an SGE job that starts IC Validator on 16 CPUs on a single host using the qsub command.

```
qsub -pe mt 16 <qsub options> icv -host_init 16 runset.rs
```

Similarly, to add 16 CPUs on one host to a running IC Validator job, use the -host\_add command-line option. For example,

```
qsub -pe mt 16  <qsub options> icv -host_add 16
```

As a convenience, the IC Validator tool can automatically determine the host configuration and sets -host\_login to qrsh -inherit . To enable this feature, specify SGE as the argument to -host\_init . In the following example, 16 CPUs are requested on a single host using qsub and are identified using the SGE argument of the -host\_init commandline option.

```
qsub -mt 16 < qsub options> icv -host_init SGE runset.rs
```

This feature is most useful when requesting jobs on multiple hosts. The following example works with multiple hosts as well (2 hosts, 16 CPUs each):

```
qsub -pe dp16 32 <qsub options> icv -host_init SGE runset.rs
```

<!-- image -->

The SGE argument also works with the -host\_add command-line option. In this example, a total of 64 CPUs are added to a running job: 8 hosts each with 8 CPUs.

```
qsub -pe dp8 64 <qsub options> icv -host_add SGE
```

To elastically add hosts to a running job, use the host\_elastic command-line option with a qsub command that requests a machine and launches IC Validator. For example, to request a single host with 8 CPUs, use the following command:

```
qsub -cwd -V -pe mt 8 icv -host_add SGE
```

Include this entire string as the argument to the host\_elastic option, or specify it in a separate script. The complete IC Validator command can look like the following:

```
icv -host_init 16 -host_elastic "qsub -cwd -V -pe mt 8 icv -host_add SGE" runset.rs
```

## Running in SLURM

When running in SLURM, the syntax and preceding examples are still appropriate. The following example shows how to launch an SLURM job that starts IC Validator on 16 CPUs on a single host using the sbatch command.

```
sbatch --cpus-per-task=16 --nodes=1 <sbatch options> run_add.sh run_icv.sh: icv -host_init 16 runset.rs (or) icv -host_init SLURM runset.rs
```

Similarly, to add 16 CPUs on one host to a running IC Validator job, use the -host\_add command-line option. For example,

```
sbatch --cpus-per-task=16 --nodes 1 <sbatch options> run_add.sh run_add.sh: icv -host_add 16 (or) icv -host_add SLURM
```

As a convenience, the IC Validator tool can automatically determine the host configuration and set -host\_login to srun with the appropriate command-line options. To enable this feature, specify SLURM as the argument to -host\_init . For example, to request 16 CPUs on a single host using sbatch :

```
sbatch --cpus-per-task=16 --nodes 1 <sbatch options> run_icv.sh run_icv.sh: icv -host_init SLURM runset.rs
```

<!-- image -->

This feature is most useful when requesting jobs on multiple hosts. The following example works with multiple hosts as well (2 hosts, 16 CPUs each):

```
sbatch --cpus-per-task=16 --nodes 2 <sbatch options> run_icv.sh run_icv.sh: icv -host_init SLURM runset.rs
```

Similarly, for adding hosts to a running job, use:

```
icv -host_add SLURM
```

To elastically add hosts to a running job, use the host\_elastic command-line option with an sbatch command that requests a machine and launches IC Validator. For example, to request a single host with 8 CPUs, use the following command:

```
sbatch --cpus-per-task=8 --nodes 1 <sbatch options> run_add.sh run_add.sh: icv -host_add SLURM
```

Include this entire string as the argument to the host\_elastic option, or specify it in a separate script. The complete IC Validator command can look like the following:

```
icv -host_init 16 -host_elastic "sbatch --cpus-per-task=8 --nodes 1 <sbatch options> run_add.sh" runset.rs
```
