## Cloud Enablement for IC Validator

This chapter explains about hybrid cloud and how to run IC Validator in a hybrid cloud environment.

The information described in this chapter is as follows:

- Overview
- Hybrid Cloud
- IC Validator Cloud Functionalities
- IC Validator on Hybrid Cloud

## Overview

Using cloud resources allows you to handle peak workloads, access powerful hardware, and scale your compute resources as needed. IC Validator supports multiple cloud service providers and integrates with hybrid environments, making it easier to manage large and complex designs.

## Using IC Validator in the Cloud

The advantages of using IC Validator in the cloud is as follows:

- Elasticity: Access virtually unlimited compute and storage resources.
- Hardware Optimization: Choose the best CPUs and GPUs for your project.
- Multi-Cloud Compatibility: Work with providers like Microsoft Azure, AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud, and HPE GreenLake.
- Pay-Per-Use: Use resources as needed and pay only for what you use.
- Seamless Hybrid Integration: Scale up with additional compute resources when required.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

- Cost-Effective Instances: Use spot instances and save-and-restore features for long jobs.
- Continuous Performance Improvements: Benefit from ongoing memory and I/O optimizations.

## Hybrid Cloud

Organizations seeking to establish or enhance a hybrid cloud environment can review various supported configurations:

## No Public Cloud Access

When cloud connectivity is unavailable, the Synopsys Cloud platform can be used to deploy a hybrid cloud environment. Refer to the Synopsys Cloud section for additional information.

## Existing Cloud Access Without Data Mirroring and Existing Compute Grid

Establishing a hybrid cloud environment requires a data mirroring service. The Synopsys Data Service offers an electronic design automation-focused alternative to third-party data mirroring solutions. Details are available in the Synopsys Data Service section.

A multi-cluster grid environment is necessary to fully leverage hybrid cloud capabilities. Consult the information technology department for guidance on configuring a multicluster grid. After assembling the required components, hybrid mode can be enabled for electronic design automation workloads.

## Existing Data Mirroring and Multi-Cluster Grid Environment

In this configuration, a data mirroring service (such as NetApp FlexCache) is already implemented, and the compute grid environment (such as IBM Load Sharing Facility or Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) supports multi-cluster operation. Most Synopsys tools operate efficiently in this environment. Tool-specific options are available for distributed execution. Refer to the Product-Specific Cloud Functionalities section for further details.

## IC Validator Cloud Functionalities

This section provides guidelines for running IC Validator in a cloud environment.

## Preparing Your Design for The Cloud

Create the runset and resolve all dependencies by copying all necessary files, including the layout database, to a local directory before transferring the design to the cloud environment.

## Note:

Refer to the IC Validator Reference Manual for detailed usage information.

## Transferring Your Design

Transferring the design files may require significant time. It is advisable to prepare a small block design first to test the cloud environment before transferring large databases. Use the small block design to verify that the runset, cloud setup, and host configurations are complete and functional in the cloud environment.

## Cloud Configuration Guidelines

## Launch IC Validator on Cloud

Run IC Validator in the cloud using standard host configurations specified on the command line. Refer to the Distributed Processing section in the IC Validator User Guide for guidance on host configuration.

Environment variable setup:

- Set ICV\_HOME\_DIR to the IC Validator installation directory.
- Set PATH to include $ICV\_HOME\_DIR/bin

IC Validator uses multiple central processing units (CPUs) on a host, as well as multiple hosts, to form a distributed job. Specify the number of hosts and CPUs for a job or allow IC Validator to determine the host pool size from the job scheduler platform, such as Load Sharing Facility (LSF) or Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management (SLURM).

Example: Submitting an IC Validator job to LSF using two hosts with 16 CPUs each:

```
bsub -n 32 -R "span[ptile=16]" <bsub options> icv -host_init LSF runset.rs
```

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Specifying LSF as the argument to -host\_init instructs IC Validator to automatically determine the host configurations and launch distributed engines to occupy two hosts with 16 CPUs each.

Additional hosts can be added to a running IC Validator job in the cloud using the -host\_add command-line option, in the same manner as with -host\_init . Hosts can also be removed from a running job by specifying them with the -host\_remove command-line option.

## Note:

Some cloud providers enforce strict memory usage policies for running jobs. Use the -host\_memory command-line option to limit IC Validator memory usage per host.

## Optimize NFS Usage on Cloud

IC Validator stores intermediate data in the group directory, typically located on a network disk under the run\_details directory. Although IC Validator automatically deletes intermediate data, the data volume may increase the cost of running IC Validator in the cloud. The following sections describe methods to reduce or eliminate IC Validator runtime network file system (NFS) footprint.

## Cache Files on Local Disk

Specify a local group directory for all hosts using the -host\_disk command-line option. In this mode, IC Validator manages file transfers among distributed hosts in the cloud. If local disk space becomes full, IC Validator stops writing to the local disk and instead uses the network path of the run\_details directory to store overflow data.

## Substitute NFS with Cloud Input/Output Layer (CIOL)

Configure IC Validator to automatically set up a CIOL mount and create a temporary network directory.

Two configurations are recommended as follows:

1. To minimize NFS usage, configure a CIOL mount for the IC Validator run\_details directory:
- Use NFS as the IC Validator job working directory to store only results and log files.
- Add the following command-line options:
- -ciol . Enables CIOL mode for IC Validator.
- -rd CIOL . Requests CIOL to create run\_details for IC Validator.
- -host\_disk /local/disk/path . Caches intermediate data on local disk to improve performance.

## 2. To run ICV without NFS usage:

- The current working directory can reside on any disk.
- Add the following command-line options:
- -ciol
- -host\_disk /local/disk/path
- Use absolute paths for all input data files in IC Validator command-line options.

To configure the CIOL data store location, set the ICV\_CIOL\_LOCAL\_DIR environment variable to a directory on disk. If this environment variable is not set, IC Validator sets up an in-memory database for CIOL data storage.

## IC Validator on Hybrid Cloud

## Distributed Processing Across On-Premises and Cloud Hosts

Running a distributed IC Validator job across both on-premises and cloud hosts requires the following prerequisites:

- A job scheduler platform capable of submitting jobs to both on-premises and cloud hosts.
- A network that allows establishing Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) connections between on-premises and cloud hosts.
- Runset files and layout databases must be accessible with identical paths on both onpremises and cloud hosts.

Two file storage configurations are recommended:

1. Use an NFS disk shared by on-premises and cloud hosts to launch IC Validator. This is the preferred configuration.
2. If a shared NFS disk is unavailable, create a shared network disk with CIOL and use it as the working directory for IC Validator. The -host\_disk command-line option is recommended for improved performance. Two options are available to configure the CIOL disk as follows:
- Launch the CIOL server first, then launch the CIOL client on all on-premises and cloud hosts to create the CIOL mount. Run IC Validator on this CIOL mount.
- Use IC Validator distributed processing to propagate the execution of CIOL clients to the hosts where IC Validator is launched.

<!-- image -->

## Note:

A -host\_login script is required when starting an IC Validator job on multiple hosts. Configure the -host\_login script to execute the CIOL client before starting IC Validator on remote hosts.

Similarly, when using the -host\_add or -host\_elastic flow, ensure that the script executes the CIOL client before starting the IC Validator executable.

## Computing on Cloud Hosts With On-Premises Data Storage

To execute an IC Validator job using only cloud hosts while keeping the runset and layout database in on-premises storage, do as follows:

1. Configure the CIOL server on an on-premises host and copy the layout and runset data to the CIOL mount.
2. Execute the CIOL client on cloud hosts before starting the IC Validator job to provide access to runset and design data.
3. After completing the IC Validator job, transfer results from the cloud to on-premises storage.

Optionally, skip the transfer step and retrieve IC Validator results from on-premises hosts by:

1. Using the CIOL mount as the working directory for the IC Validator job.
2. Using the -host\_disk command-line option for improved performance.
3. Executing the CIOL client with the on-premises host to monitor the running IC Validator job and review the results.

<!-- image -->

## 4

## Output Files

This chapter provides an overview of IC Validator design rule checking (DRC) and layoutversus-schematic (LVS) output files.

The information described in this chapter is:

- Description of Output Files
- General DRC and LVS Output Files
- LVS-Specific Output Files

## Description of Output Files

The output files produced by the IC Validator tool are specific to the type of run performed. If you are performing DRC, the tool produces error and summary files. The error files list the DRC errors in your design. The summary files list information about your design and the completed run.

If you are performing device extraction, the IC Validator tool produces error, summary, and layout netlist files. The layout netlist file is the file that is compared to a schematic netlist during LVS comparison. Both DRC and device extraction runs produce tree structure, virtual cell, and technology files in the run\_details and run\_details/hierarchy directories.

If you are performing LVS comparison, the IC Validator tool produces error, log, and equivalence summary files. The error file lists the nets and devices from the layout that do not match the schematic.

The error, summary, and layout netlist files are written to current working directory. There are additional files, which are located in the run\_details directory, that help in debugging LVS errors.

All output files are named cell .abbreviation, where cell is the name specified by the cell argument in the library() function. The extension following cell is an abbreviation for the explanation of the file. For example, the account file name is cell .acct.

<!-- image -->

## General DRC and LVS Output Files

Figure 4 shows the output files and directories common to both DRC and LVS runs. The files are described in the following sections.

Figure 4 Output Files and Directories Common to DRC and LVS

<!-- image -->

## Results File

The IC Validator tool creates a RESULTS file, cell .RESULTS, that provides the results from key areas of the run and a summary of the search and grep key results. The RESULTS file also contains the IC Validator command line options used for the run. This file is the starting point for analyzing the results of an IC Validator run.

<!-- image -->

The cell .RESULTS file is divided into the following sections:

- Results Header

If the DRC run completed with no violations, the IC Validator tool returns a single line that states, 'RESULTS: CLEAN'.

If the DRC run completed, but with violations, the IC Validator tool returns a single line that states, 'RESULTS: NOT CLEAN'.

If the LVS run completed, the IC Validator tool returns two results in the header section:

- The first result is a single line that states, 'LVS Compare Results: PASS | FAIL'.
- The second result is a single line that states, 'DRC and Extraction Results: CLEAN | NOT CLEAN'.

A DRC or LVS run that does not complete returns a single line that states, 'RESULTS: RUN ABORTED'.

- Execution

This section consists of two parts:

- The first part prints the IC Validator banner and copyright information, and how the IC Validator tool was called.
- The second part consists of basic run information, which includes the following items: input library file name, top cell name, layout format of input library, runset file name, working directory path, run details directory path, LVS error file name, layout error file name, user name, and start and end time of the IC Validator run.
- Results Summary: DRC Run

This section consists of two parts:

- The first part reports the rule and DRC error statistics, including the total number of rules that are run, the number of rules that are not executed, the number of rules that contain violations, and the total number of violations. See the cell .LAYOUT\_ERRORS file for detailed violation data.
- The second part consists of a table showing each rule name and the total number of violations found for that rule. This part is output only if the verbose\_results\_file argument of the run\_options() function contains the ERRORS option. Rule names are extracted from rule comments based on the rule\_name\_delimiter argument of the error\_options() function. If you run DRC error classification, the number of waived violations is excluded from the number of violations found. Any rule that was not executed shows a 'Not Executed' status. Violation counts for individual functions under a rule are not reported, with the

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

exception of functions without a rule. These functions are reported (indented by two spaces) under the default rule name, 'Violation.' Violation counts are preceded with the 'v =' string for easy searching of a specific violation count.

- Results Summary: LVS Run

This section consists of two parts:

- The first part is the table of LVS compare statistics. This section reports the following LVS compare statistics: LVS compare results, top equivalence points, number of checked black-box cells, number of passed black-box cells, number of failed black-box cells, number of checked equivalences, number of successful equivalences, and number of failed equivalences. See the cell .LVS\_ERRORS file for the detailed compare violation data.
- The second part lists the LVS results of all equivalence and black box pairs; the first being the failed equivalences and black-box cells, followed by passed equivalences and black-box cells. You can search or grep the list to quickly find the results of equivalence and black-box cells.
- Assign Layer Statistics

This section consists of two parts:

- The first part reports four items: total number of used assign layers, number of empty used assign layers, number of non-empty used assign layers, and number of pruned assign layers.
- The second part consists of a table showing each layer name, hierarchical and flat polygon counts for the layer (or 'Pruned' if the layer was pruned), and the layer or datatype assignments for the layer. This part is output only if the verbose\_results\_file argument of the run\_options() function contains the ASSIGNS option.

The table is divided into three sections: 1) non-empty used layers 2) empty used layers 3) pruned layers. The assign statement for each layer contains layer datatype assignments and all other user-supplied assignment options.

- Run Configuration

This section consists of the following seven parts:

- The run\_options() function reports the verbose\_results\_file argument.
- The hierarchy\_options() function reports the delete argument.
- The error\_options() function reports the following items: error\_limit\_per\_check , match\_errors , report\_empty\_violations , and clean\_classifications arguments.

<!-- image -->

- The drc\_black\_box\_options() function reports the following items: black\_box\_cells , black\_box\_region\_cells , keepout\_layers\_check , and keepout\_violation\_comment arguments.
- Production Environment Variables report all production environment variables that are set. A total count of these environment variables is printed at the end of the list.
- Debug Environment Variables report all debugging environment variables that are set. A total count of these environment variables is printed at the end of the list.
- Distributed processing reports the distributed cores and turbo, followed by a list of host machines with their specifications (model name, CPU, cores, RAM, swap space). Each host machine also displays the number of distributed processes and the number of CPU on the host next to the host name.
- Performance Statistics

This section reports five items:

- IC Validator runtime
- Peak single command memory
- Peak disk usage
- Distributed host peak memory usage (this is a table showing each host, the distributed processing and number of CPU on that host, and the host peak memory and RAM)
- Overall distributed utilization

## Error File

The IC Validator tool creates an error file, cell .LAYOUT\_ERRORS, during DRC or netlist extraction runs. These types of errors are referred to as layout errors. The LAYOUT\_ERRORS file contains the results of a run, a summary list of the errors, and a more detailed list of the errors.

The top of the file states either CLEAN or ERRORS so that you can quickly determine if there are layout errors in the design.

The next section is the summary section. This section provides the comment for a function, the function itself, and the number of errors for that function if it had errors.

The last section is the details section. Each error report contains the following: an error description that identifies the check being performed; a structure name where the error occurred; a position or a bounding box value where the error occurred; and other information specific to a check. The position coordinates are reported hierarchically, that is, relative to the named structure and only one time for each referenced structure. These errors can also be viewed graphically using the VUE debugging tool.

<!-- image -->

During the run, the LAYOUT\_ERRORS file is kept up-to-date with the results and the summary sections. At the end of the run, a final version of the file is written including the details section, as specified by error\_options(report\_error\_details) .

The following section of the LAYOUT\_ERRORS file shows a minimum area rule for metal1 (Met1). The rule was coded as follows in the runset:

```
//R.Met1.A { area( Met1, value < 0.04);
```

```
@"R.Met1.A:For Metal 1, minimum area must be 0.04"; }; The LAYOUT_ERRORS file reports this rule as follows: LAYOUT ERRORS RESULTS: ERRORS ##### ####  ####   ###  ####   ### #     #   # #   # #   # #   # # ####  ####  ####  #   # ####   ### #     #  #  #  #  #   # #  #      # ##### #   # #   #  ###  #   # #### ========================================================================= Library name:    ../../lab_data/INLIB_TRAINING.GDS Structure name:  top Generated by:   IC Validator <platform> <release> <date> Runset name: icv runset.rs User name: juser Time started: 2016/03/02 07:35:12AM Time ended: 2016/03/02 07:35:51AM Called as: icv runset.rs ERROR SUMMARY R.Met1.A: Minimum area must be 0.04 area .............................................. 1 violation found. ERROR DETAILS -------------------------------------------------------------------------R.Met1.A: Minimum area must be 0.04 -------------------------------------------------------------------------sf.rs:238:area - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -Structure ( lower left x, y ) ( upper right x, y) Area
```

```
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -top       (37.2700, 4.0300)   (37.4800, 4.1700)   0.0294
```

## Summary File

The IC Validator tool creates a summary file, cell .sum, during DRC or netlist extraction runs.

If you are using the -verbose command-line option, the information printed to the screen is the same as the information reported to the summary file. The screen output, however, prints the information in the order of processing by the IC Validator tool, while the content of the summary file sorted to match the sequential order of the runset.

## Rules File

Rules to be executed are written to the cell .rules file in the run\_details directory. Violation names and violation comments that remain in the runset after all forms of runset selection have been performed are reported in the cell .rules file. Examples of runset selection include preprocessor directives, selectable rules, incremental layers, and run-only pruning.

Violation names and violation comments are harvested for all rules in the final parse tree. Because runtime conditional commands ( if / then / else statements and for / foreach / while loops) might remain, rules in the final parse tree are not guaranteed to execute. Rule output is included for all commands in the final parse tree, including commands that do not execute due to runtime conditions.

Violation names and violation comments might not always be statically resolved. In this case the file and line number are provided in the output file instead of the rule name.

Only the violation comment is present in the output if there is no '@=' violation block for the runset rule.

The default comment is 'Violation' and '@ \'Violation\'' appears in the rules to be output when a rule uses the default comment.

The following is an example cell .rules file:

```
ICV_Master (R) Copyright (c) 1996 - 2015 Synopsys, Inc. This software and the associated documentation are proprietary to Synopsys,Inc. This software might only be used in accordance with the terms and conditions a written license agreement with Synopsys, Inc. All other use, reproduction, or distribution of this software is strictly prohibited. Called as: icv runset.rs -i test.gds - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
```

```
User name:        synopsoid
```

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

```
Layout format:    GDSII Input file name:  test.gds Top cell name:    top Time started:     2015/11/03 02:43:08PM -------------------------------------------------------------------------Rules to be Executed -------------------------------------------------------------------------Unresolved violation name/comment found at runset.rs:100 @ "Rule comment with no violation block" @ "Violation" VIOL_101 @= { @ "VIOL_101_comment" } VIOL_102 @= { @ "VIOL_102_comment" } VIOL_103 @= { @ "VIOL_103_comment" } VIOL_104 @= { @ "VIOL_104_comment" } VIOL_105 @= { @ "VIOL_105_comment" }
```

## Technology File

The IC Validator tool creates a technology file, cell .tech file, that displays the options which are set for the IC Validator run. The list of options includes the default as well as the userspecified values. The technology file contains three sections: exploded cells, deleted cells, and placement explode statistics.

## Tree Structure Output File

The IC Validator tool creates tree structure files, named cell .tree, during DRC or netlist extraction runs. Tree structure files contain information about the design hierarchy tree and reference statistics for every cell in the design tree. The cell .tree0 file represents the original data. The cell .tree1 file is created after all of the exploding options are completed. Additional tree files are created when using the hierarchy options. The cell .tree N file with the highest number ( N ) is the hierarchy that was processed during the run. The tree files are printed if the print\_preprocess\_files argument of the run\_options() function specifies the TREE option, the compress\_tree\_files argument is used to determine if the tree files are compressed when written to disk.

## Virtual Cell File

The virtual cell file, cell .vcell, contains information about pairing, creating sets, and exploding of virtual cells depending on the options you use in the IC Validator runset and the data in your design. It includes the Pair, Set, and Exclude sections.

## Pair Section

The Pair section reports the cell pairs that were created during each virtual cell pass iteration. The iterate\_max option of the pairs argument of the hierarchy\_options() function sets the maximum number of iterations.

## Set Section

The Set section reports the sets that were created during each virtual cell pass iteration. The iterate\_max option of the sets argument of the hierarchy\_options() function sets the maximum number of iterations.

## Explode Section

The Explode section of the output file displays all of the branches that were exploded to bring together interacting placements under a common parent. For more information, see the explode argument of the hierarchy\_options() function in the IC Validator Reference Manual .

## Distributed Log File

The distributed log file, named with the runset name and a dp.log extension, contains more information than a summary file, as it includes details about when a function is sent to a host, and the results produced when the host completed the function. The distributed log file is in order of execution rather than in order of the runset.

## Distributed Statistics File

A distributed statistics file, named with the runset name and a dp.stats extension, contains distributed processing statistics.

## Distributed Work Directory

A distributed work directory, named dp\_work, is created for a distributed run in the run\_details directory. The directory contains subdirectories and files used during the distributed run. If this directory exists before a run, it and all of its content are deleted and new files are created. Because this directory is deleted before the run, do not name any individual directories dp\_work in the run\_details directory of a run.

## Graphical Error Structures

The IC Validator tool generates an error database, PYDB, that can be viewed in a layout editor, such as VUE. It contains error polygons and coordinates that are located in proximity to design rule violations. The shapes produced by different checks can be written to separate layers and data types in the error structure, as specified in the runset file. See DRC Error Classification, for a description of the error database and of the pydb\_report and pydb\_export utilities that you can use to classify errors.

The error database contains all the error data generated by violation blocks and all the information needed for a VUE debugging session. By default, this database is in run\_details/pydb. You can change the location by using the db\_path argument of the error\_options() function. This database allows for data mining, and you can create custom reports.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Note:

You can start reviewing the error database before the IC Validator tool completes the run.

The IC Validator tool generates a hierarchy of error structures that mimics the database hierarchy that is being checked. Thus, any errors that are found in a particular structure in the database appear in a corresponding error structure in the error hierarchy. Error structures are generated only for the database structures that contain errors or that reference other structures with errors. The IC Validator tool does not create an error hierarchy if no errors were found.

Error structures are named with the default error prefix, ERR\_. This prefix precedes the structure name. For example, the default error structure for the cell CLOCK is ERR\_CLOCK. You can redefine the error prefix using the error\_cell\_prefix argument in the write functions, such as the write\_gds() function.

For example,

| Database hierarchy                                  | Error hierarchy                                                            |
|-----------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| CHIP { ALU { BIT0 BIT1 } CLOCK { CLK1 CLK2 CLK3 } } | ERR_CHIP { ERR_ALU { ERR_BIT0 ERR_BIT1 } ERR_CLOCK { ERR_CLK1 ERR_CLK3 } } |

In the error hierarchy, there is no occurrence of the error structure ERR\_CLK2. Either the original CLK2 cells were exploded during preprocessing, or the structure CLK2 did not contain any errors or structures that contain errors. If a previous IC Validator run with errors is corrected and rerun, previous error hierarchy structures are retained. The IC Validator tool does not overwrite these structures if no errors are found, but the new error hierarchy does not have references to these previous error containing cells.

## LVS-Specific Output Files

Figure 5 shows the output files and directories for LVS runs. The files are described in the following sections.

<!-- image -->

Figure 5 Output Files and Directories for LVS

<!-- image -->

## LVS Debugging File

The compare() function creates a debugging file, cell .LVS\_ERRORS, that indicates whether or not the schematic-versus-layout comparison was successful. This file is the starting point for debugging LVS issues.

Depending upon whether the comparison was successful or not, the file lists the PASS/ FAIL information and layout errors if any. The LVS\_ERRORS file then lists the important failed equivalence points, sorted in high and low priorities, and provides diagnostics designed to assist you in troubleshooting the design.

## Extracted Layout Netlist File

The IC Validator tool creates an extracted layout netlist file, cell .net, whenever a netlist() extraction function is specified in the runset file. This file is a hierarchical description of the structures found in the layout database.

## Extracted Layout SPICE Netlist File

The IC Validator tool creates an extracted SPICE layout netlist file, cell .sp, whenever the write\_spice() function is specified in the runset file. This file is a hierarchical SPICE description of the structures found in the layout database. See the write\_spice() function in the IC Validator Reference Manual for further information.

## Account File

The IC Validator tool creates an account file, cell .acct, that lists the number of devices and their types extracted from each cell in the hierarchy. The cumulative count shown is the total count of all devices contained in that structure.

## Bounding Box File

The IC Validator tool creates a bounding box file, cell .bbox, that lists the total number of cells and the bounding box coordinates of each cell in the design.

## Equivalence Files

If you do not supply an equivalence file, then an LVS compare run automatically produces an equivalence file that is used to compare the layout and schematic netlists. When producing an equivalence file, the IC Validator tool recognizes that some equivalence points are extraneous and do not aid in the comparison process. After all analysis is completed, the IC Validator tool generates an equivalence file, equiv.run, that lists all the equivalence cells that were used during the run. See the equiv\_options() function in the IC Validator Reference Manual for more information.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Device Leveling Summary File

The device leveling summary (DLS) file gives you a way to trace how a device was extracted in terms of hierarchy level. You can determine the root cause of why a device was extracted at the wrong level of hierarchy (that is, leveled) by the diagnostic information in the cell .dls file, which is in the run\_details directory.

The following is an example cell .dls file.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ |                        ICV Device Leveling Summary                    | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ Device Leveling Summary Results: Body Layers          | Cell | Layer Interacted: ----------------+--------+---------------------ngt.polygonlayer.0001  A      nsd.polygonlayer.0001, NW.polygonlayer.0003 pgt.polygonlayer.0001  B      psd.polygonlayer.0001 ...
```

The device leveling summary file shows body layers for devices that cannot be pushed back to their original cells after device recognition and property calculations. The device body layers that are successfully pushed back are not shown in this file. The file shows

- Body Layers. Derived layer of device body that is leveled out of the cell in which it originally resides.
- Cell. Original cell of the leveled devices.
- Layer Interacted. Layer that interacted with device body, causing device leveling. If there is an interaction among body layer polygons from the same body layer across multiple levels of hierarchy, the body layer name is printed in this column.

## Compare Log File

The IC Validator tool creates a log file, cell \_lvs.log, during an LVS run. This compare log file contains all of the messages related to the compare() function.

## Compare Tree Files

The compare() function produces two tree files. One is named lay.tree; it provides the hierarchical structure of the layout netlist. The second is named sch.tree; it provides the hierarchical structure of the schematic netlist. These files are in the run\_details/lvsflow directory.

<!-- image -->

## Compare Directory Output Files

The detailed output files from an LVS comparison are placed in the compare directory run\_details/compare. A subdirectory of this compare directory is created for each equivalence point in the equivalence file as the equivalence points are evaluated. These subdirectories are named based on the layout structure name. Figure 6 shows an example of a compare directory.

Figure 6 Compare Directory Structure Example

<!-- image -->

## Individual Equivalence Summary File

The results of the comparison of each structure are written to a summary file named sum. schematic\_module\_name . layout\_structure\_name , generally referred to as the sum. cell . cell file. The file is located in the compare subdirectory of the working directory, as shown in Figure 6. This file is not generated if the remove\_equiv\_sum\_files argument of the compare() function is NONE or if the particular equivalence point is completed without errors or warnings. The information in the summary file includes the following: the number of occurrences of each device found; the total number of nets that were found; and the number of devices and nets that were removed or created by merging. If all of the devices and nets could not be matched, the summary includes a listing of the discrepancies.

The sum. cell . cell file is divided into the following sections:

- Comparison Result
- Diagnostic Error
- Unmatched Nodes
- Error Information

- Warning Information
- Preprocessing Information
- Comparison Information
- Merged Node Information
- Cross-Referencing Information
- Statistics Report

## Partitioned Schematic Netlist

The schematic data used for this portion of the comparison process is written to the sch. cell file. This file is located in the compare subdirectory of the working directory, as shown in Figure 6. This file is not generated if the write\_equiv\_netlists argument of the compare() function is FAILED and the particular equivalence point is completed without errors or warnings, or if the argument is NONE . This file is the schematic netlist that results after exploding nonequivalent structures; it generally provides little or no useful information for analyzing comparison results.

## Partitioned Layout Netlist

The layout data used for this portion of the comparison process is written to a file called lay. cell . This file is located in the compare subdirectory of the working directory, as shown in Figure 6. However, this file is not generated if the write\_equiv\_netlists argument of the compare() function is FAILED and the particular equivalence point is completed without error or warnings, or if the argument is NONE . This file is the layout netlist that results after exploding nonequivalent structures; it generally provides little or no useful information for analyzing comparison results.

## Editing Errors

After the error structure has been placed into the database, you can begin editing and correcting the errors. The LAYOUT\_ERRORS file lists the location and the structure name for each error encountered. The summary file, cell .sum, lists the checks that have errors.

Because the output of the IC Validator tool is hierarchical, you need to correct an error only one time, no matter how many times the structure is placed. You continue this process until all errors are eliminated.

<!-- image -->

## IC Validator Dashboard

This chapter describes the IC Validator Dashboard capabilities.

The IC Validator Dashboard is described in the following sections:

- Introduction
- Getting IC Validator Dashboard Email Updates From IC Validator
- Starting IC Validator Dashboard Standalone
- The IC Validator Graphical User Interface

## Introduction

IC Validator Dashboard provides an easy way for you to see how a run is progressing, how many rules exist and how many have completed, how many violations have been reported, and how IC Validator is using the resources it has been allocated.

As chips near completion, physical verification runs are in the critical path for tapeout, and it becomes increasingly important to ensure they complete on time. IC Validator Dashboard can be used effectively together with the IC Validator -host\_elastic , -host\_add , and -host\_remove command-line options to help you optimize your physical verification runs and hardware resources.

## Getting IC Validator Dashboard Email Updates From IC Validator

IC Validator Dashboard can send you updates by email. IC Validator sends them automatically based on the percentage of completed updates written to the icv.log file. You can enable these updates by specifying -email dashboard on the IC Validator command line when you start the run. For example:

```
icv ... -email dashboard ... runset.rs
```

The emails contain the three pages of content, in which IC Validator Dashboard shows an MRI snapshot colored by memory usage, and a heat map of violation density.

<!-- image -->

Figure 7 IC Validator Dashboard Email Contents

<!-- image -->

## Starting IC Validator Dashboard Standalone

You can start the IC Validator Dashboard using the following command:

```
icv_dashboard [-email ["user1,user2,..."]] [-V] [-h] [<run_details_path>|<dp_log_file>]
```

If you do not provide any arguments, Dashboard looks for a distributed processing log file in the ./run\_details directory and opens the graphical user interface (GUI).

The command-line options are described in Table 23.

| Option                   | Description                                                                   |
|--------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| -email ["user1,user2,…"] | Sends a single email update to the user and exits.                            |
| -V                       | Prints the product version and exits. Other command-line options are ignored. |
| -h                       | Prints program options and exits. Other command-line options are ignored.     |

Table 23 IC Validator Dashboard Command-Line Options

<!-- image -->

Table 23 IC Validator Dashboard Command-Line Options (Continued)

| Option                            | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| run_details_path&#124;dp_log_file | Displays the GUI using either the specified run details directory or the DP log file. The default is ./run_details/. When the run details directory is specified, the distributed processing log file in that directory is used. If more than one distributed processing log file exists in that directory, the log file to use must be specified explicitly. |

## Note:

To start IC Validator Dashboard in this way, ensure that your PATH variable contains $ICV\_HOME\_DIR/bin, and that either LM\_LICENSE\_FILE or SNPSLMD\_LICENSE\_FILE environment variables point to a valid Synopsys license server with an IC Validator license.

## Initial Directory Setting

The IC Validator Dashboard automatically creates an initial directory to store intermediate files. You can specify a path for the initial directory by setting the environment variable, DASHBOARD\_TMP . If this path is set and valid, then the IC Validator Dashboard creates the initial directory in this path, otherwise the current directory is the next choice, followed by your home directory. If the IC Validator Dashboard fails to create the initial directory, an error is shown.

## The IC Validator Graphical User Interface

When you start the GUI is started interactively using the command-line options described in the previous section, it continuously monitors the IC Validator run it found or was pointed to. The GUI opens displaying the Summary page which, after it has loaded the information from the run, displays the contents in Figure 8.

## IC Validator Dashboard Summary Page

The Summary page shows five panels, which provide information on the status, CPU usage, memory usage, run progress, and rule progress. You can see additional information about the rule progress or status 'lights' by hovering the pointer over them until the tooltip appears.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Figure 8 IC Validator Dashboard Summary Page

<!-- image -->

Figure 9 IC Validator Dashboard Status Panel

<!-- image -->

## IC Validator Dashboard Status

There are five IC Validator Dashboard status values:

- Waiting

This is shown when IC Validator Dashboard GUI has started and is waiting for the IC Validator run to start and the distributed processing log file to appear.

- Running

Shown while the IC Validator run is running and IC Validator Dashboard is waiting for an update.

- Completed

Shown when the IC Validator run has completed successfully.

- Stopped

Shown when the IC Validator run has ended with an error

<!-- image -->

- Unknown

Shown when IC Validator Dashboard has read an incomplete distributed processing log file, but cannot tell if the job is still running. This can occur if a partial distributed processing log file has been loaded when IC Validator is no longer running.

## IC Validator Run Status Indicators

In general, these status indicators are green. When IC Validator is short on disk space or memory, the respective indicator turns red. The 'Other' status indicator turns red if a command has crashed, a host has been dropped, or if a significant portion of the total runtime is consumed by deferred commands. Hover the pointer over the indicator to display the reason for the status.

## IC Validator Run Information

This section of the status panel displays the primary inputs to IC Validator.

## CPU Usage Panel

The CPU usage panel shows the total CPUs in use across all hosts for the IC Validator run. When you run IC Validator in elastic mode, some CPUs might be released while the job is running. In that case, it is possible for the peak usage to exceed the allocated CPUs.

Figure 10 IC Validator Dashboard CPU Usage Panel

<!-- image -->

## Memory Usage Panel

The Memory Usage panel shows the memory usage of the host using the most memory. When more than one host is allocated to the IC Validator run, this might change throughout the course of the run.

## IC Validator Live DRC

This appendix discusses the IC Validator Live DRC tool usage within the Custom Compiler, IC Compiler II, Fusion Compiler, and Cadence Virtuoso tools.

The IC Validator Live DRC tool is described in the following sections:

- About the IC Validator Live DRC Tool
- IC Validator Live DRC With Custom Compiler
- IC Validator Live DRC With Virtuoso
- IC Validator Live DRC With IC Compiler II and Fusion Compiler

## About the IC Validator Live DRC Tool

Long DRC runtimes on advanced nodes and large designs can affect productivity. The IC Validator Live DRC tool enables you to run DRC directly within a layout editor, helping you fix violations actively and eventually generate a much cleaner layout that reduces signoff DRC runtime.

The IC Validator Live DRC tool uses the IC Validator signoff rule file so that the checks are comprehensive. However, because you are limiting the checks to the viewport and visible layers only, the runtime is significantly faster. The IC Validator Live DRC tool is supported within the Custom Compiler™, IC Compiler™ II, Fusion Compiler™, and Cadence® Virtuoso® Layout Editors.

## IC Validator Live DRC With Custom Compiler

IC Validator Live DRC in Custom Compiler allows designers to run IC Validator physical verification checks on active layouts. IC Validator Live DRC allows you to get instant DRC results using the same runset and files as IC Validator. Advanced options like recipes allow you to create subsets of rules which can be selected and executed from a pull-down menu. For better ease of use, the violations are displayed within Custom Compiler without the need for a separate window to view violations. The following sections describe the steps to set up IC Validator Live DRC, execute a run, and view violations.

<!-- image -->

## Additional Options

Additional options like halos and recipes allow you to better control the run. For example, halos expand the data that is being checked to include some area immediately outside the view window and recipes allow you to create and run subsets of rules that can be selected from a pull-down menu.

## Halos

To run IC Validator Live DRC on data that is immediately outside the data in the view window, add a halo to the run. Adding a halo increases the size of the check window, as shown in Figure 27. By expanding the data checked to include the polygons immediately outside the view window, you can verify that design changes within the view window did not create any new DRC violations with the polygons immediately outside the view window.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Figure 27 IC Validator Live DRC Configuration - Halo Size

<!-- image -->

The black window is the viewport and the red window is the viewport plus the halo. If IC Validator Live DRC is executed with the halo setting:

- Only polygons that have some portion of their area inside the red window are included in the check. (Polygon 1 is included, but Polygon 2 is not).
- Only error shapes that overlap the black window are included in the result (Error 1 included, but Error 2 is not).

You can define the halo range using IC Validator Live DRC by specifying the xtICVLiveHaloRange preference. You can control whether IC Validator Live DRC writes out two OA markers to indicate the checking range by specifying the xtICVLiveDumpCheckingRange preference, in which case one marker shows the checked viewport, and the other marker considers the halo range.

## Recipes

Recipes are JSON text files that contain a subset of rules from the signoff runset. Recipes allow you to run specific rules based on the design stage. For example, a recipe containing spacing rules or rules related to front-end layers can be executed at the very early stages of a design. Recipes with more advanced rules or rules related to back-end layers can be executed toward the end of the design cycle. You can create new recipes or modify existing recipes by setting the Recipe File path, which contains multiple recipes that can be defined using the Recipe Editor .

## To invoke the Recipe Editor :

<!-- image -->

1. From the Live DRC Setup dialog box, Main tab, select an existing Recipe File and click , as shown in Figure 28, to load the Recipe Editor . R
2. Click , as shown in Figure 28, to choose a recipe from the Select Recipe File dialog box. Click OK to load the Arguments field with the selected recipe.
3. Choose &lt;No-Recipe&gt; , as shown in Figure 29, to remove the recipe settings from the Arguments path and create a new recipe.

<!-- image -->

Figure 28 Recipe Editor With Arguments

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

4. Check or uncheck the rules from the Rule Name list that you want to be included in your recipe. Click to save a new recipe or the settings of an existing recipe. Click to remove the existing recipe of the specified Recipe File. X
1. Capture the coordinates of your run from the Console:
2. Create a config.rs file in your run directory using the following lines, and substitute the arguments in select\_window with the coordinates of the IC Validator Live DRC run from the previous step:

Figure 29 Recipe Editor

<!-- image -->

```
hierarchy_options( explode_all = {"*"} ); incremental_options( select_window={{-4.444, -5.012, 188.725, 47.064}}, clip_window=false, window_error_filter = KEEP_ENCLOSED );
```

IC Validator Live DRC runs on flat data. Therefore, you must use the hierarchy\_options() function to flatten the input to the IC Validator run. Although IC Validator Live DRC does not clip polygons at the edge of the view window, it does not report any violations outside of the view window. Therefore, the clip\_window and

<!-- image -->

```
window_error_filter arguments must be used with the incremental_options() function.
```

3. Add this file to your IC Validator run by setting -runset\_config config.rs .
4. Run IC Validator.

## IC Validator Live DRC With Virtuoso

IC Validator Live DRC in Virtuoso allows you to run IC Validator physical verification checks on active layouts. IC Validator Live DRC allows you to get instant DRC results using the same runset and files as IC Validator. Advanced options like recipes allow you to create subsets of rules which can be selected and executed from a pull-down menu. Violations are displayed within Virtuoso without the need for a separate window to view violations. The following sections describe the steps to set up IC Validator Live DRC, execute a run, and view violations.

## Setting Up the Environment

To set up IC Validator Live DRC with Virtuoso, some environment variables must be set so the IC Validator installation can be located by IC Validator Live DRC.

1. Set up the environment

Set the ICV\_HOME\_DIR environment variable to the location where IC Validator is installed.

Set the SYNOPSYS\_SYSTYPE environment variable appropriately for your system. Typically, it should be set to linux64.

Start Virtuoso, and in the CIW window type,

```
load( strcat( getShellEnvVar("ICV_HOME_DIR") \ "/etc/icvlive/virtuoso/icvl.il"))
```

Alternatively, this command can be added to the .cdsinit file to automatically load the IC Validator Live DRC toolbar in Virtuoso.

## Additional Options

Additional options like halos and recipes allow you to better control the run. For example, halos expand the data that is being checked to include some area immediately outside the view window and recipes allow you to create and run subsets of rules that can be selected from a pull-down menu.

## Halos

Adding a halo increases the size of the check window, as shown in Figure 37. By expanding the data checked to include the polygons immediately outside the view window, you can verify that design changes within the view window did not create any new DRC violations with the polygons immediately outside the view window.

Figure 37 IC Validator Live DRC Configuration - Halo Size

<!-- image -->

The black window is the viewport and the red window is the viewport plus the halo. If IC Validator Live DRC is executed with the halo setting:

- Only polygons that have some portion of their area inside the red window are included in the check. (Polygon 1 is included, but Polygon 2 is not).
- Only error shapes that overlap the black window are included in the result (Error 1 included, but Error 2 is not).

## Check Layers

The Check Layers option controls which rules to include when checking according to visible layers. The available options are shown in Figure 38.

Figure 38 IC Validator Live DRC Configuration - Check Layers

<!-- image -->

The various options are as follows:

- All Layers : Includes all rules to check
- Visible Layer Only : Includes rules using visible layers only
- Visible Layer Involved : Includes rules that have at least one visible layer involved

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

For example, consider the following three rules and assume only VIA is visible:

```
Rule1 @= { @ "Rule1"; area(VIA, value = [2.0,2.0]); } Rule2 @= { @ "Rule2"; VIA and M1; } Rule3 @= { @ "Rule3"; M1 and M2; }
```

When All Layers is selected, Rule1, Rule2, and Rule3 are included.

When Visible Layer Only is selected, only Rule1 is included.

When Visible Layer Involved is selected, both Rule1 and Rule2 are included.

## Honor the P&amp;R Boundary visibility

The Honor the P&amp;R Boundary visibility option is effective when Check Layers is set to Visible Layer Only or Visible Layer Involved .

When the option is not set, the P&amp;R Boundary object is always treated as visible.

When the option is set, Live DRC honors the visibility the P&amp;R Boundary object on the Virtuoso editor.

Figure 39 IC Validator Live DRC Configuration - Honor the P&amp;R Boundary visibility

## Saving and Loading Configurations

Configuration files allow you to save the runset and other settings used in an IC Validator Live DRC run. Saving the settings allows you to get back to your work even when a previous session is closed and a new layout or session is opened. Configuration files are JSON-based text files similar to the IC Validator Recipe files. This section describes how to create and load these files to your IC Validator Live DRC run. To load a configuration file before you run, set the ICV\_LIVE\_CONFIG\_FILE followed by the file or directories separated by colons. For example,

```
setenv ICV_LIVE_CONFIG_FILE file1:/path/to/dir1:file2:$cwd
```

You can edit any files that have write permissions directly from the IC Validator Live DRC Configuration Window.

After you set up a configuration, you can save it by clicking the save button and using the pop-up dialog.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

If this configuration is commonly used, it might be useful to load it automatically. You can do this with the ICV\_LIVE\_CONFIG\_FILE environment variable. Set this to a colon separated list of files or directories. When the IC Validator Live DRC configuration menu is opened, IC Validator Live DRC reads the configuration files in the ICV\_LIVE\_CONFIG\_FILE path. You can then select a configuration from the configuration drop-down list at the top of the Configuration menu.

Figure 45 User Configuration

<!-- image -->

Add the runset and the layer map. The configuration drop-down menu displayed at the top of the Configuration window can be used to switch between different configuration settings.

## Saving Configurations

To save configurations:

1. In the ICV Live Configuration , click OK or Apply .
2. Switch to another configuration using the Configuration drop-down list.
3. Click the Create Configuration or Load Configuration file.

Figure 46 Saving Configurations

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Figure 47 Create Configuration

<!-- image -->

- IC Validator Live DRC checks the write permissions of the configuration as follows:
- a. If the unsaved configuration is writable, IC Validator Live DRC saves changes into a writable configuration file.
- b. If the unsaved configuration is read-only, a message appears to prompt you to save the configuration in a new writable configuration file or overwrite an existing writable configuration file.

## Contents of a Configuration File

A configuration file is written in JSON format. The configuration files in IC Validator Live DRC are designed to remember the initial user settings in subsequent new sessions. One configuration file can have multiple configurations. For example, an N7 configuration file might have two configurations - one for BEOL runs and one for FEOL runs.

## For example:

```
%vi n7_configurations.icvlc { "configurations": [ { "checkFilter": { "checkLayers": "Visible Layers Involved", "excludeDensityRules": true, "loadedRecipeFiles": [ "/path/to/beol_spacing.icvrcp", "/path/to/beol_density.icvrcp" ], "selectedRecipe": "Spacing Rules", "selectedRecipeFile": "/path/to/beol_spacing.icvrcp" },
```

<!-- image -->

```
"name": "BEOL Configuration", "runSettings": { "clfFile": "/path/to/beol_clf.txt", "enableColoring": true, "exportLayoutToOasis": true, "haloSize": 1.5, "layerMappingFile": "n7.layermap", "objectMappingFile": "n7.objmap", "runsetFile": "n7.rs" } }, { "checkFilter": { "checkLayers": "All Layers", "excludeDensityRules": true, "loadedRecipeFiles": [ ], "selectedRecipe": "", "selectedRecipeFile": "" }, "name": "All Layers ", "runSettings": { "clfFile": "", "enableColoring": false, "exportLayoutToOasis": false, "haloSize": 1, ], "selectedRecipe": "Custom Checks", "selectedRecipeFile": "/path/to/feol.icvrcp" }, "name": "FEOL Configuration", "runSettings": { "clfFile": "/path/to/feol_clf.txt", "enableColoring": true, "exportLayoutToOasis": true, "haloSize": 1.5, "layerMappingFile": "n7.layermap", "objectMappingFile": "n7.objmap", "runsetFile": "n7.rs" } } ], "majorVersion": 1, "minorVersion": 0 }
```

## Preference Settings

Live DRC stores preference-related settings into a per-user file. These settings do not affect a Live DRC check but affect GUI and highlighting.

For example, the Highlight Control section is stored as preference.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

By default, this information is stored to $HOME/.synopsys/icvlive/prefs.icvlc .

To change the file that you want to store, set the ICV\_LIVE\_PREF\_FILE followed by a file name.

For example, setenv ICV\_LIVE\_PREF\_FILE /path/to/my\_prefs.icvlc

## Run Directory

Set the \_ICV\_LIVE\_CLIENT\_ENABLE\_GUI\_RUN\_DIR environment variable to enable the Run Directory field as shown in Figure 50. Use this field to specify the directory where Live DRC writes the intermediate files. If you do not specify a directory, Live DRC saves the intermediate files to $HOME/.synopsys/icvlive by default.

Figure 50 Run Directory Field In Preference Settings

<!-- image -->

To override the GUI setting, set the ICV\_LIVE\_OUTPUT\_DIR environment variable. This environment variable has a higher priority than the Run Directory field in the GUI.

## Bindkeys

IC Validator Live DRC bindkeys allow for quick access to common functions. There are two default bindkeys that can be written at the end of the icvl.il file, which is located in $ICV\_HOME\_DIR/etc/icvlive/virtuoso/icvl.il .

- Shift+F12 brings up the config window.
- F12 runs IC Validator Live DRC.

<!-- image -->

You can define bindkeys by using the hiSetBindKey() function to set the Layout, Key, and SKILL function to call, as shown here:

- Fill icvlSetup(hiGetcurrentWindow()) to bring up the config window.
- Fill icvlExecute(hiGetCurrentWindow()) to run IC Validator Live DRC.
- Fill icvlBrowse(hiGetCurrentWindow()) to bring up violation viewer.

## For example:

```

```

## IC Validator Live DRC With IC Compiler II and Fusion Compiler

You can perform interactive signoff design rule checking in the IC Compiler II or Fusion Compiler GUI using the IC Validator Live DRC tool.

## Setting Up the Environment

To perform interactive signoff design rule checking using IC Validator Live DRC,

1. Set up the IC Validator environment. Specify the location of the IC Validator executable by setting the ICV\_HOME\_DIR environment variable. You can set this variable in your .cshrc file. To specify the location of the IC Validator executable, use commands similar to those shown in the following example:

```
setenv ICV_HOME_DIR /root_dir/icv set path = ($path $ICV_HOME_DIR/bin)
```

You must ensure that the version of the IC Validator executable that you specify is compatible with the IC Compiler II or Fusion Compiler version that you are using. To report the version compatibility, use the report\_versions IC Compiler II or Fusion Compiler command.

2. Set the application options for interactive signoff design rule checking.

At a minimum, you must specify the foundry runset to use for design rule checking by setting the signoff.check\_drc.runset application option and the layer mapping file that maps the technology file layers to the runset layers by setting the signoff.physical.layer\_map\_file application option.

<!-- image -->

Before you run interactive design rule checking, configure the run by setting the application options for interactive signoff design rule checking, as shown in Table 24. To set the application options, use the set\_app\_options command. To see the current settings, use the report\_app\_options command.

| signoff.check_drc_live.default_h alo           | 1                          | Specifies the distance in microns by which to expand the region in which IC Validator Live DRC performs checking.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

By default, IC Validator Live DRC keeps only those violations that are fully within the checking region. ## Displaying Objects for Design Rule Checking

When you run interactive design rule checking, the IC Validator tool performs design rule checking on what is displayed in the layout window, plus an extension of 1 micron.

You can modify the size of the extension by setting the signoff.check\_drc\_live.halo application option. Use the View Settings and Hierarchy Settings panels to control the layers, levels, and cell types displayed in the layout window.

- Display the View Settings panel by clicking the View Settings icon in the panel area.
- Specify the number of levels to display in the Level field.
- Select the Layers tab and enable visibility for the required layers.
- Display the Hierarchy Settings panel by clicking the Hierarchy Settings icon in the View Settings panel or the menu bar.
- Specify the number of view levels in the 'View level' field.
- Select Standard, 'Fill Cell,' and Block in the 'Expanding cell types' section.

## Setting Up Pre-Compiled Cache Directories

The IC Validator Live DRC feature recompiles the runset each time it detects new layers in the view window or when the rule selection changes. If you change the view windows and visible layers frequently, this can cause frequent compilations, which can slow down the IC Validator Live DRC runtime. To improve performance, prepare a cache directory containing cache files generated during the design process. When the window changes in the future, the IC Validator Live DRC feature can search for and reuse an older cache file from this directory if the layers, rule-selection, and settings match the current run. These cache directories can be shared with other users. To create runset cache directories and reuse or share files:

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

1. Set up the local cache directory and run IC Validator Live DRC to compile the runset with different configurations.
2. Transfer the cache files from &lt;first\_user local&gt; to the &lt;new\_user&gt; shared cache directory, &lt;new\_user shared&gt;.
3. Set up both local and shared cache directories in &lt;new\_user&gt; to run IC Validator Live DRC so that it can pick up the precompiled files as well as store newly created cache files in the local path.

```
unset ICV_DISABLE_RUNSET_CACHE setenv ICV_RUNSET_CACHE_DIR <first_user local> // Start ICV Live
```

```
unset ICV_DISABLE_RUNSET_CACHE setenv ICV_RUNSET_CACHE_DIR <new_user local> setenv ICV_RUNSET_CACHE_DIR_SHARED <new_user shared> // Start ICV Live
```

<!-- image -->

IC Validator Live DRC runs on flat data. Therefore, you must use the hierarchy\_options() function to flatten the input to the IC Validator run. Therefore, the clip\_window and window\_error\_filter arguments must be used with the incremental\_options() function.

3. Add this file to your IC Validator run by setting -runset\_config config.rs .
4. Run IC Validator.
