## IC Validator Explorer DRC

This chapter explains the IC Validator Explorer DRC capabilities.

IC Validator Explorer DRC is described in the following sections:

- Introduction to IC Validator Explorer DRC
- Types of Explorer DRC Modes
- Configuring Explorer DRC
- Explorer DRC Output Files
- Debugging With Explorer DRC
- Explorer DRC Licenses

<!-- image -->

## Introduction to IC Validator Explorer DRC

Debugging DRC violations early in the design process can be complex and time consuming. For example, complicated DRC rules (multiple patterning and delta voltage) run for a very long time and do not add value when other simpler violations exist.

A basic set of design checks can be used to debug typical early design issues: finding cell overlaps, improper fill, and routing issues does not require complicated rules. IC Validator Explorer DRC automatically determines these basic rules from the foundry runset. It also adds extra methodology rules and debugging capabilities. This results in a significant reduction in turnaround time.

In addition, IC Validator Explorer DRC detects when design layers flag too many violations and deselects related slow-running rules. Such dynamic selection and execution of checks achieves a faster turnaround time than traditional full DRC runs.

## Types of Explorer DRC Modes

There are three Explorer DRC modes:

- Explorer DRC Standalone Mode

This mode runs automatically selected design rules from the foundry runset and IC Validator-added methodology checks.

Use the standalone mode for designs with violations that require fast checking with low computing resources.

- Explorer DRC Tiers Mode

Explorer DRC tiers provide a systematic framework for executing and reporting the high-priority checks first. In the tiers mode, checks are completed regardless of performance. All rules are selected and executed based on the tier order and up to the specified tier.

Performance is not the main consideration when you use this mode.

Some tiers are reserved for Explorer priority rules and methodology checks. Most of the tiers however, are user-customizable. See Table 26 for more information.

The tiers are executed in order of assigned priorities. Lower-numbered tiers have the highest priority. Undefined checks between Tier 0 and Tier 10 are executed after Tier 10, as part of an 'All remaining rules' tier. Results are updated during the run, as each tier finishes.

## Example of Running in Tiers Mode

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

```
Run Explorer DRC auto mode on all Tiers with User defined Tiers specified using -explorer_tiers_file mytier.txt % icv -explorer auto -explorer_tiers_file mytier.txt runsetfile
```

## · Explorer DRC Auto Mode

Similar to the tiers mode, this mode also uses the Explorer DRC tiers. However, this mode also has the ability to stop slow-running rules.

When design layers with violations are found in auto mode, related rules are stopped if their functions are slow-running. This allows for results from earlier tiers to be used to stop later functions/rules from running too long (rules from tier 0 and tier 1 are never stopped early).

The performance of this mode depends on the number of DRC errors. The larger the number of DRC errors, the more likely it is that auto mode deselects rules and exits early to achieve a faster turnaround time.

Use the auto mode when the number of violations in the design is unknown and you want to complete as many checks as possible. If the design is clean, auto mode does not stop any of the checks, and it produces full signoff results.

## Executing Explorer DRC

```
To execute Explorer DRC, set -explorer standalone|auto[: TierNumber ]| tiers[: TierNumber ] on the command line,
```

where TierNumber specifies the highest tier to be executed.

All tiers up to and including TierNumber are executed. If TierNumber is not specified, all of the checks are candidates for execution.

See the following section on configuring IC Validator Explorer DRC for more information.

## Examples of Running in Explorer DRC Mode

```
Run Explorer DRC standalone mode % icv -explorer standalone runsetfile Run Explorer DRC auto mode up to Tier 4 % icv -explorer auto:4 runsetfile
```

Table 26 shows the different Explorer DRC tiers, pre-included checks, and customizable categories.

Table 26 Explorer Tiers

| Tier    | Can the user add checks to this tier?   | Can the user name this tier?   | Included checks                                                 | Optional checks                 |
|---------|-----------------------------------------|--------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------|
| 0       | No                                      | No                             | Methodology warnings, fill overlap diagnostics, priority rules, | N/A                             |
| 1       | Yes                                     | No                             | None                                                            | Priority rules (user-specified) |
| 2       | Yes                                     | Yes                            | Voltage-based diagnostics (set 1)                               | User-specified rules            |
| 3       | Yes                                     | Yes                            | Voltage-based diagnostics (set 2)                               | User-specified rules            |
| 4 to 10 | Yes                                     | Yes                            | None                                                            | User-specified rules            |
| N/A     | N/A                                     | N/A                            | All remaining rules                                             | N/A                             |

## Configuring Explorer DRC

The Explorer DRC mode command-line options are described in Table 27.

Table 27

Explorer DRC Mode Command-Line Options

| Option                                                                   | Definition                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| -explorer standalone&#124;auto[: TierNumber ]&#124; tiers[: TierNumber ] | Runs Explorer mode with either standalone , auto , or tiers mode. TierNumber is optional for the auto and tiers modes to limit the run up to TierNumber specified. If not specified, all of the tiers are candidates for execution.                                          |
| -explorer_tiers_file path_to_file                                        | Specifies the file to customize so that user-defined tiers can be passed to the Explorer DRC run. The ADD_RULES_TO_TIER and NAME_TIER directives can be used in this file.                                                                                                   |
| -explorer_script path_to_file                                            | Specifies the file used to add resources after Tier 0 and Tier 1 are completed. You can start an auto run with fewer resources and dynamically add resources when Tier 0 and Tier 1 are completed. Use these resources for a faster turnaround time of the remaining checks. |

The -explorer\_tiers\_file path to file command-line option points to an optional script file that you can use to customize tiers. An example of this file might look like the following:

```
ADD_RULES_TO_TIER 1 "*.1:" "*G1*" ADD_RULES_TO_TIER 2 "*.S.*" "**DN*"
```

<!-- image -->

```
NAME_TIER 4 "Handoff Rules" ADD_RULES_TO_TIER 4 "*delta*" ADD_RULES_TO_TIER 4 "*LU*" DISABLE EXPLORER.OVERLAP
```

The following directives can be used to create this file:

## · ADD\_RULES\_TO\_TIER TierNumber Rule comment … Rule comment

Use this directive for tiers that allow user-specified rules. You can add rules to the tiers based on the violation comments. String matching is supported.

Rules are added to tiers in ascending priority order. If a rule has already been added to a higher priority tier, it is not added to any lower priority tiers. This rule applies regardless of the order of specification in the Explorer tiers file.

Skipped or empty tiers are allowed. When Explorer DRC encounters an empty tier, execution moves to the next priority tier. Reporting is in tier priority order.

## · NAME\_TIER TierNumber TierName

Use this directive for tiers that allow a user-specified name. This name is used when reporting to the LAYOUT\_ERRORS file, RESULTS file, or VUE.

Unnamed tiers are allowed. They are reported with the default Explorer tier name, TierNumber .

## · DISABLE\_EXPLORER.DiagnosticName

Use this directive to disable Explorer proprietary diagnostics. The supported values are:

- EXPLORER.OVERLAP . Disables fill overlap diagnostics that are included by default in Tier 0.
- EXLORER.ASSIGN . Disables assign-layer based priority rules that are included by default in Tier 0.
- EXPLORER.VOLTAGE . Disables voltage-based diagnostics that are included by default in Tier 3 and Tier 4.

The -explorer\_script path\_to\_file command-line option runs after both the Tier 0 and Tier 1 checks are completed. You can start DRC auto mode with fewer resources than necessary to complete the entire run. If more resources are needed to run additional tiers, this command-line option adds additional resources following the basic checks. An example of a script file looks like this:

```
#!/bin/csh -f echo "Explorer Tier 0 and Tier 1 checks are done. Adding resources and running remaining Tiers"
```

<!-- image -->

```
# Following command adds host "A" to ongoing run icv -rd run_details -host_add A
```

## Explorer DRC Output Files

Explorer DRC creates ASCII files that are similar to an IC Validator DRC run. See Output Files for more information on DRC run files.

In both the LAYOUT\_ERRORS and RESULTS files, errors from an Explorer run are categorized in Table 28.

Table 28 Explorer Error Categorization

| Category                      | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Methodology warnings          | Specifies Explorer methodology warnings aimed to flag potential design or performance issues.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Fill overlap diagnostic       | Specifies DRC errors that are diagnosed as fill overlap issues (runset selected fill overlap rules).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Priority rules                | Specifies DRC errors that are available from Explorer priority checks (runset selected basic rules).Some of the rules in this category might get an EXPLORER prefix, which denotes that the rule has been modified (faster version) from the original runset. The original runset version runs as part of DRC Errors in the 'All remaining rules' category. |
| Priority Rules (user-defined) | Specifies DRC errors available from user-defined priority rules.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Voltage dependent diagnostics | Specifies Explorer methodology warnings that flag text-based voltage conflicts on polygons or net objects. In addition, stray voltage texts and voltage checks are included.                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Explorer tier TierNumber      | Specifies DRC errors from unnamed tiers. By default, these errors are categorized under Explorer tier, TierNumber . You can modify the tier name using the NAME_TIER directive in the file.                                                                                                                                                                 |
| All remaining rules           | Specifies the available DRC errors from checks that are classified as predefined or user-defined tiers.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

In addition to the error categorizations in Table 28, DRC errors are categorized by their user-defined category names (defined using the NAME\_TIER directive in the file).

## Note:

Error categories are dependent upon the type of Explorer mode and diagnostics flagged in that mode.

<!-- image -->

## Explorer DRC Results File

Explorer DRC creates the RESULTS file, cell.RESULTS. This file provides results from the run and also the IC Validator command-line option used for the run.

The RESULTS file is used as the starting point for analyzing the results of an Explorer DRC run. The Results summary section reports the DRC error statistics, as categorized in Table 28. Statistics include the total number of rules and violations in the different Explorer categories.

## Explorer DRC Errors File

Explorer DRC creates a LAYOUT\_ERRORS file, which provides layout errors that are flagged during the run. These errors are categorized in Table 28.

To ensure the error report is concise, error coordinate information is suppressed in the LAYOUT\_ERRORS file. This is equivalent to running error\_options (report\_error\_details = false) . The information is stored in the error database (PYDB), but only the violation summary section is written to the LAYOUT\_ERRORS file.

The LAYOUT\_ERRORS file is generated after each tier/category so that you can reference it during the Explorer DRC run. The icv.log file indicates when a tier/category is completed, as follows:

```
ICV_Engine run is 5% complete. Elapsed Time=0:07:24 All Priority Rules are finished! 19103703 violations were found.
```

## Note:

While storing error markers in the error database (PYDB), Tier 0 and Tier 1 (Explorer priority checks and user-defined priority checks) enforce the limit set by the error\_sampling\_per\_check argument (the default is 1 million). The limit of other tiers is based on the runset. See the IC Validator Reference Manual for more information about the error\_sampling\_per\_check argument.

## Explorer DRC VUE File

IC Validator Explorer creates the VUE file, cell.vue, to view Explorer DRC error details and the Heat Map.

<!-- image -->

## Debugging With Explorer DRC

To analyze an Explorer DRC run,

1. Run IC Validator with Explorer DRC.
2. Review the RESULTS file.
- If the results are clean, go to signoff DRC. If the results are not clean, go to step 3.
3. Load the Explorer DRC .vue file into VUE. Attach the layout editor to VUE.
4. Click the Heat Map tab to start debugging. The Error Heat Map is a graphical interface used to visualize error distributions.

Heat Maps are automatically enabled for Explorer DRC. See the 'Introduction to the IC Validator Error Heat Map' chapter in the IC Validator VUE User Guide for more information.

5. Similar to the RESULTS and LAYOUT\_ERRORS files, the Explorer DRC errors are categorized by default in Table 28. In general, start debugging in order from methodology warnings, diagnostics, predefined priority rules, user-defined tiers and, finally, to all remaining rules.

In addition, you can select the Clustered Errors category mode from the menu in the Violation Category window. In this mode, identical errors are clustered together so that multiple rules can be debugged at one time. See the 'Introduction to the IC Validator Error Heat Map' chapter in the IC Validator VUE User Guide for more information on clustered errors.

6. After rules are selected from their respective categories, isolate the areas with a high number of error counts (red regions in the heat map) and zoom into these dense regions.
7. Probe the heat map and layout errors in these regions to analyze the underlying cause for the high error count. Probing might include:
- Zooming into regions
- Highlighting error markers in those regions
- Selecting or deselecting specific rules
8. Repeat steps 6 and 7 until all categories/clusters are exhausted.

<!-- image -->

## IC Validator Explorer LVS

This chapter explains the IC Validator Explorer LVS capabilities.

- Introduction to IC Validator Explorer LVS

## Introduction to IC Validator Explorer LVS

Finding the root cause of LVS errors early in signoff LVS is critical in reducing the overall signoff period and meeting a tapeout schedule. Explorer LVS targets the System-On-Chip (SOC) full chip, and provides a solution where you can find the root cause of LVS issues with a quick turnaround time and efficient machine resources. This reduces the overall signoff time and effort.

Explorer LVS focuses initially on LVS issues that stem from SOC integration, and then gradually expands its analysis to cover other potential LVS issues, such as LVS errors from the device or base layers or cells in the lower hierarchy.

To check the issues from SOC integration, by default, Explorer LVS performs a text-based short check with only the equivalence cells and metal layers that make up the SOC Top (for example, P&amp;R, PowerGrid, placeholder polygon fill cells that build up the main SOC structure, as opposed to macros and IPs that are instantiated underneath the main SOC structure, and so on). The scope of checking LVS issues can be expanded as needed using flexible options provided by Explorer LVS.

Explorer LVS helps increase the productivity and efficiency of signoff LVS. It does not replace the traditional LVS tool. Final signoff LVS must run with the traditional LVS tool.

<!-- image -->

## Executing Explorer LVS

To execute Explorer LVS, set -explorer lvs on the command line. This commandline option takes the AUTO , METAL , or SHORTS defaults of the -explorer\_lvs\_cells , -explorer\_lvs\_layers , or -explorer\_lvs\_checks command-line options. Explorer LVS performs text-based short checks on the SOC Top cells with only metal layers.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## The default behavior can be altered with the three Explorer LVS options

-explorer\_lvs\_cells , -explorer\_lvs\_layers , and -explorer\_lvs\_checks , as described in Table 29.

Certain cells specified with -explorer\_lvs\_preserve\_cells can be preserved from being deleted or black-boxed in Explorer LVS so that those cells can be included in Explorer LVS.

SeeTable 30 for examples of how to execute Explorer LVS.

Table 30 Examples of Executing Explorer LVS

| Mode                                           | Command Line                                                                          | Description                                                                                                               |
|------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Default                                        | % icv -explorer lvs \ runsetfile                                                      | Text-based short checks on the SOC Top cells with metal layers only                                                       |
| Add all of the cells to the default            | % icv -explorer lvs \ -explorer_lvs_cells ALL \ runsetfile                            | Text-based short checks on all of the cells with metal layers                                                             |
| Add all of the layers to the default           | % icv -explorer lvs \ -explorer_lvs_layers ALL \ runsetfile                           | Text-based short checks on the SOC Top cells with all of the layers                                                       |
| Add all of the cells and layers to the default | % icv -explorer lvs \ -explorer_lvs_cells ALL \ -explorer_lvs_layers ALL \ runsetfile | Text-based short checks on all of the cells with all layers                                                               |
| Add LVS compare check to the default           | % icv -explorer lvs \ -explorer_lvs_checks ALL \ runsetfile                           | Text-based short checks along with LVS compare on the SOC Top cells with metal layers only                                |
| Preserve CellA and CellB in Explorer LVS       | % icv -explorer lvs \ -explorer_lvs_preserve_cells \ "CellA CellB" runsetfile         | Same as the default behavior with the only difference being where Explorer LVS guarantees CellA and CellB to be preserved |

## Explorer LVS Licenses

IC Validator Explorer LVS requires Elite licensing. This feature requires the following IC Validator licenses:

ICValidator-Manager

ICValidator2-GeometryEngine See the Licensing and Resource Requirements chapter in the IC Validator User Guide for more information.

## 9

## PXL

This chapter describes PXL, a programmable and extensible language, as well as the basics of function definitions and the use of functions in the IC Validator tool.

PXL is described in the following sections:

- PXL Architecture
- General Definitions
- Variables and Operators
- Data Types and Typing
- Flow Control
- Functions
- Program Structure
- Example of Modularized Code

<!-- image -->

## PXL Architecture

PXL is fully programmable, with general programmability features such as

- Variables
- Flow Control
- Lists (arrays) with standard indexing
- Structures
- Hashes
- Enumerated types
- User-defined functions
- Mathematical, logical, and string operations
- Macros with command-line option support
- Environment variables
- Static scope

These features allow for

- Straightforward runset development
- Easy to maintain runsets
- Succinct code
- Code reuse with subroutines
- Support user-defined functions

Figure 55 shows the basic structure of PXL.

<!-- image -->

Figure 55 PXL Structure

<!-- image -->

## General Definitions

This section provides definitions and characteristics of some syntactic elements in PXL, such as identifiers, string literals, keywords operators, and comments. Understanding the purpose and function of syntactic elements is helpful while creating runsets.

## Identifiers

Identifiers for any PXL components can include alphabetic characters, numbers, and underscores in any order.

PXL is case-sensitive. The identifiers listed here are all different:

- abCD
- ABCD
- abcd

<!-- image -->

## The following naming restrictions apply to identifiers:

- Two leading underscores (\_\_). Identifiers with two leading underscores are not allowed. They are reserved for internal language use.
- One leading underscore (\_). Identifiers with one leading underscore are not allowed. They are reserved for product use.
- All uppercase. Reserved for use by the application programming interface. You can, however, use uppercase identifiers as enumerated type elements.
- Reserved keywords. Reserved keywords must not be used as identifiers. For a list of reserved keywords in PXL, see Keywords on page 189.'

You cannot use these names as identifiers:

- Function names: The functions are defined in the IC Validator Reference Manual and the IC Validator header files. Example function names are capacitor, check\_property, internal1, and xor.
- Container type names: These names of lists, hashes, and structures are defined in the IC Validator header files. Here are some examples of container type names:
- Lists: coordinate\_l is used in defining the property() function
- Hashes: layer\_list\_h is used in defining the density() function
- Structures: check\_property\_s is used in defining the check\_property() function

## Examples of valid identifiers are

```
This IsAnIdentifier another_identifier_using_underscores layer20
```

## Examples of reserved (invalid) identifiers are

```
__SYSTEMNAME (Two leading underscores; reserved for internal language usage) _productname (One leading underscore; reserved for product use) HIERARCHICAL (Reserved keyword)
```

<!-- image -->

## String Literals

A string literal is a group of characters beginning and ending with a double quotation mark ( " ).

## Note:

The first character of a text string cannot be an integer or a space followed by an integer.

String literals must not contain a new line. If a new line is needed in a string literal, the new-line character ( \n ) must be used.

The following groups of characters are examples of string literals:

```
"hello" "\"" "a string with\nmultiple lines" "abc" "def"
```

String literals are automatically merged con ate i f s r g with any adjacent string literals. In particular, they are merged with preprocessor variables that contain string values, such as \_\_FILE\_\_ , as well as references to environment variables, such as $&lt;id&gt; .

Use escape sequences within strings to set aside parts of the string as instructions to the compiler. The available set of escape sequences in PXL are shown in Table 31.

Table 31 Escape Sequences

| Escape   | Definition                         |
|----------|------------------------------------|
| \n       | New-line character                 |
| \"       | Double quotation mark character    |
| \\       | Single backslash character         |
| \ NNN    | Octal value of the character       |
| \ t      | Tab character                      |
| \x NN    | Hexadecimal value of the character |

## Numeric Constants

Numeric constants in PXL are defined as shown in Table 32.

<!-- image -->

Table 32 Numeric Constants

| Number type        | Condition                                                                             | Example         |
|--------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------|
| double             | Contains an exponent.                                                                 | 4e5, 10.305e+10 |
| double             | Contains a decimal.                                                                   | 3.141592        |
| decimal integer    | Contains a leading numeral (1-9).                                                     | 1023            |
| octal number       | Contains a leading zero (0) and any of the digits from zero (0) to seven (7).         | 0346            |
| hexadecimal number | Contains a leading 0x or 0X, and can contain only the hexadecimal digits (0-9a-fA-F). | 0xDEADBEEF      |

## Keywords

Keywords are built-in words that are recognized by the language. Keywords are reserved and therefore cannot be used as identifiers.

A few of the uses of keywords are

- Flow controllers, such as if , foreach , and while
- Operators, such as in and contains
- Constants, such as true and false

The following tables list the res v d k ywo reserved words in PXL.

See Identifiers on page 186' for more information about naming restrictions.

| deprecated | intrinsic   | method     |
| obsolete   | preprocess  | primary    |

| shutdown   | unsafe      | unique     |

## Operators

Operators are symbols that have a particular meaning. For example, + indicates that two numbers are added. The operator types are shown in Table 37.

| Operator type       |   Number of arguments | Example                          |
|---------------------|-----------------------|----------------------------------|
| unary unary ope t   |                     1 | Logical not (!)                  |
| binary binary ope t |                     2 | Addition (+) Exponentiation (**) |
| ternary terna y op  |                     3 | Question operator (e1 ? e2 : e3) |

Table 37 Operator Types

## Comments

Comments are text used to document the program. Comments are useful in indicating the intent of the code to readers. Comments are treated as white space. The comment types, shown in Table 38, are based on how many lines each comment contains.

Table 38 Comment Types

| Comment type   | Starts with   | Ends with     | Length     |
|----------------|---------------|---------------|------------|
| line           | //            | Next new line | One line   |
| block          | /*            | */            | Any length |

Block comments do not nest. If */ is seen within a comment, the preprocessor reports a warning. For example, if the runset contains

```
/*      - 1st comment start /*      - 2nd comment start */      - 2nd comment end */      - 1st comment end
```

The "1st comment start" matches with "2nd comment end"; the "1st comment start" does not match with "1st comment end".

Here are some examples of comments:

```
/* this is a single-line block comment */ // this is a line comment, so /* is ignored /* block comments /* cannot nest. Therefore this comment evokes a warning from the preprocessor */ /* * block comments can span * several lines, such * as this one does. */ /* A leading * is not required on each line of a block comment but does make the comment stand out from the program. */
```

<!-- image -->

## Environment Variable Reference

Environment variables are a set of dynamic values that can be used to control the way processes are run.

Environment variable references have the dollar sign character ($) followed by any normal identifier. If an undefined environment variable is referred to, it is rejected with a compiletime error.

Environment variables are replaced by a string literal containing the value of the environment variable. Replacement is only done on tokens of the form $&lt;id&gt;. Specifically, there is no replacement within string literals; replacement is not required because adjacent string literals are concatenated.

## Note:

If the value of the environment variable is an empty string, it is converted to a string literal whose value is an empty string.

Here are some examples of environment variable usage:

```
x : string = $y; /* * assuming environment variable my_value contains the value abcd, * the following code evaluates to true; otherwise evaluates to false. */ res : boolean = ( $my_value == "abcd" ); /* * if environment variable aaa contains the value * /home/dir/path, the following code produces a string * containing a path to the file "cases" in that directory. */ path : string = $aaa "/cases"; /* * if environment variable bbb is defined but empty, the * following code produces the string abcdef. */ mystr : string = "abc" $bbb "def";
```

## Variables and Operators

This section introduces the concepts of variables and operators in PXL.

<!-- image -->

## Variables

Variables are used to store information temporarily in the program.

When declaring variables, the variable name must be followed by a colon (:) and the variable type. Variables can also be given an initial value when declared. See the examples in the following section.

## Note:

See the Identifiers section for information about naming restrictions.

## Initializing Variables

You can initialize variables to any of the supported data types in two ways:

```
· Using a literal value. y : boolean = true;           // initialize by literal value · Using an expression. z : boolean = !y;             // initialized by expression
```

The following examples show different methods of initialization:

```
x : integer;                     // no initial value pi : double = 3.141592;          // initialized by value pi2 : double = pi * 2;           // initialized by expression s : string = "abc" "def";        // concatenated s1 : string = "abc" + pi;        // converted to string,then concatenated c : constraint of double = (10.0,200];  // initialized by value
```

## Scope of Variables

Scope in PXL is the meaning that variables and expressions have within several contexts in a program. The various rules and conditions that relate to scope of variables are described here by using examples.

Local scope is defined by a set of braces ({ }). That is, compound statements, defined with curly braces, define a new variable scope. See Compound Statement on page 241 for the use of braces.

Flow control statements create a new scope.

```
if ( var == 1) {         // Start of new scope my_var: integer = 1;
```

<!-- image -->

```
... }                       // End of scope.
```

- Variables declared in a local scope do not exist outside of that scope. That is, if a variable is declared inside of a particular scope, the variable cannot be used outside of that scope. For example,
- Variables are global from outermost scope to innermost scope. For example,
- Variables declared in an outer scope that are redeclared in an inner scope are shadowed to prevent value collisions.
- If variable shadowing occurs and the scope of the shadowed variable is not defined by a function declaration, the program generates a warning.
- Within function calls, shadowing is expected and there is no warning. For example,

```
{ x = y + b; } z = x;      // x is not defined; it only exists in the local scope
```

```
{ x : integer = 1; { a = x + b;  // x exists and can be seen within this scope // (global from  outer scope) x = y + b;  // global value of x is overwritten } z = x;         // x is defined here and contains the value of y + b } z = x;            // x is not defined here - parser error
```

```
y: integer = 1; x: integer = 1; { y : integer = 3;  // The original y value is shadowed. // This is a new y. x = x + 1;        // x is equal to 2 here y = y + 1;        // y is equal to 4 here } // y is equal to 1 here - the shadowed value // returns when exiting the inner scope // x is equal to 2 here
```

Here is another example of variable shadowing. The function declaration:

```
fxy : function ( x : integer; y : integer; ) returning z : integer { x = x + 1; y = y + 1;
```

<!-- image -->

```
z = x + y; };
```

## The function call:

```
x1 : integer = 1; y : integer = 1; z1 = fxy(x1, y);  // within the function y is shadowed // y in the local scope is "2" x2 = x1;          // x1 is "1" y1 = y;           // y is still "1" z2 = z1;          // z1 is "4"
```

## Operators

operat s, d fin Operators are symbols used within an expression to specify certain operations that are to be performed while evaluating that expression.

PXL supports the following operators:

- Assignment Operators
- Relational Operators
- Logical Operators
- Conditional Operator
- Numeric and Bitwise Operators
- Operators With Double-Only Outputs

## Assignment Operators

An assignment operator evaluates an expression and saves it to a target lvalue.

An lvalue is an expression that can contain a value and can be used on the left side of an assignment statement.

Assignments involving the use of &gt; or &gt;= in constraint values must have white space before and after the assignment operator. You can also place the constraint value within parentheses following the assignment =.

For example,

```
abc = >=3; xyz = (>5);
```

<!-- image -->

## Note:

Assignment operators cannot cascade. This example is not legal:

```
a = b = c
```

The following examples show proper assignment:

```
x:   integer;  // declare a variable named x point: newtype struct of { x: integer; y: integer; }; // declare a struct // of integers p: point; x   = 42;      // assign x a value of 42 p.x = 10;      // assign p.x a value of 10 p.y = 27;      // assign p.y a value of 27
```

## Relational Operators

A relational expression evaluates an expression to a Boolean value, either true or false.

Table 39 defines the relational operators.

Table 39 Relational Operators

| Syntax   | Description                                        | Supported for                     |
|----------|----------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| e1 == e2 | true if e1 is equal to e2, false otherwise         | All completely defined data types |
| e1 != e2 | true if e1 is not equal to e2, false otherwise     | All completely defined data types |
| e1 < e2  | true if e1 is less than e2, false otherwise        | Numbers                           |
| e1 <= e2 | true if e1 is not greater than e2, false otherwise | Numbers                           |
| e1 >= e2 | true if e1 is not less than e2, false otherwise    | Numbers                           |
| e1 > e2  | true if e1 is greater than e2, false otherwise     | Numbers                           |

## Logical Operators

A logical expression evaluates to a Boolean value. A logical operator requires that all arguments to be of boolean type. Expressions are evaluated from left to right, and stop when the result is defined. Table 40 defines the logical operators.

## Table 40

Logical Operators

| Syntax   | Description                         |
|----------|-------------------------------------|
|          | if e1 is false, then false, else e2 |

```
e1 && e2
```

<!-- image -->

Table 40 Logical Operators (Continued)

| Syntax             | Description                          |
|--------------------|--------------------------------------|
| e1 &#124;&#124; e2 | if e1 is true, then true, else e2    |
| ! e1               | if e1 is true, then false, else true |

## Conditional Operator

A conditional expression takes three arguments; the first argument must be of boolean type. Table 41 defines the conditional operator.

Table 41 Conditional Operator

| Syntax   | Description                     |
|----------|---------------------------------|
| e1 ? e2  | if e1 is true, then e2, else e3 |

Consider a conditional operator with three arguments e1, e2, and e3. The conditional operator is evaluated in the following order:

1. The first argument (e1) is evaluated.
2. If the first argument (e1) evaluates to true, the second argument is evaluated.
3. If the first argument (e1) evaluates to false, the third argument (e3) is evaluated.

## Numeric and Bitwise Operators

All standard mathematical operators are supported in PXL. The bitwise operators are supported only for integers. Table 42 defines the numeric and bitwise operators.

| Syntax   | Description       | Allowed for        | Comments                                         |
|----------|-------------------|--------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| e1 + e2  | Addition          | Integer and double | Returns a double if either argument is a double. |
| e1 - e2  | Subtraction       | Integer and double | Returns a double if either argument is a double. |
| e1 * e2  | Multiplication    | Integer and double | Returns a double if either argument is a double. |
| e1 % e2  | Integer remainder | Integer and double | Returns a double if either argument is a double. |

Table 42 Numeric and Bitwise Operators

<!-- image -->

Table 42 Numeric and Bitwise Operators (Continued)

| Syntax   | Syntax    | Description                            | Allowed for   | Comments   |
|----------|-----------|----------------------------------------|---------------|------------|
| e1       | << e2     | Logical left shift (zeros shifted in)  | Integer       |            |
| e1       | >> e2     | Logical right shift (zeros shifted in) | Integer       |            |
| e1       | & e2      | Bitwise AND                            | Integer       |            |
| e1       | &#124; e2 | Bitwise OR                             | Integer       |            |
| e1       | ^ e2      | Bitwise XOR                            | Integer       |            |
| !        | e1        | Bitwise NOT                            | Integer       |            |

## Operators With Double-Only Outputs

Division ( / ) and exponentiation ( ** ) treat the arguments as doubles and always return only doubles. Table 43 defines these operators.

Table 43 Operators With Double-Only Outputs

| Syntax   | Description    | Accepts            | Comments                                                                   |
|----------|----------------|--------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| e1 / e2  | Division       | Integer and double | e1 and e2 are forced to be doubles. The operation always returns a double. |
| e1 ** e2 | Exponentiation | Double             | e1 and e2 are forced to be doubles. The operation always returns a double. |

## Note:

Any expression with a division operator (/) or exponentiation operator (**) cannot be used as the index of a list or hash table.

To perform an integer operation, you must wrap the operation in a call of the dtoi() function. This function converts a double into an integer. For example,

```
var : integer = dtoi(10/3);
```

<!-- image -->

## Member Reference

A member reference expression accesses one member of a compound object. The member reference takes the type of that single member. The member is an lvalue and functions as the target of an assignment. Table 44 defines member reference expressions. See Assignment Operators on page 208.' for more information about lvalue.

Table 44 Member Reference

| Syntax   | Description                         |
|----------|-------------------------------------|
| e1 . e2  | Structure member access by name     |
| e1 [ e2  | List or hash member access by index |

## Precedence and Associativity

Table 45 lists the precedence and associativity of all operators in PXL. The top of the table is the highest precedence, and the bottom is the lowest.

Table 45 Precedence and Associativity of Operators (Highest Precedence First)

| Operators       | Associativity                   |
|-----------------|---------------------------------|
| () [] .         | Left to right                   |
| **              | Right to left (exponentiation)  |
| ! + -           | Right to left (unary operators) |
| == != < <= > >= | Illegal (unary operators)       |
| * / %           | Left to right                   |
| + -             | Left to right                   |
| << >>           | Left to right                   |
| < <= > >=       | Non associative                 |
| == !=           | Non associative                 |
| &               | Left to right                   |
| ^               | Left to right                   |
|                 | Left to right                   |

|

<!-- image -->

Table 45 Precedence and Associativity of Operators (Highest Precedence First) (Continued)

| Operators              | Associativity   |
|------------------------|-----------------|
| &&                     | Left to right   |
| &#124;&#124;           | Left to right   |
| ?:                     | Right to left   |
| = @= ?=                | Illegal         |
| User-defined operators | Non associative |

Table 46 defines each type of associativity.

## Table 46 Associativity

| Associativity   | Definition                                                                             |
|-----------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Left to right   | Expressions are evaluated from left to right.                                          |
| Right to left   | Expressions are evaluated from right to left.                                          |
| Non associative | Parenthesis are required.                                                              |
| Illegal         | The operator does not cascade. Operators do not produce the same type as they consume. |

The following examples show how associativity works:

```
/* * pairs of expressions show evaluation order */ A + B + C ( A + B ) + C A ** B ** C A ** ( B ** C ) A * B + C >> 2 ( ( A * B ) + C ) >> 2 A >= B == C ( A >= B ) == C A < B == C > D ( A < B ) == ( C > D )
```

<!-- image -->

## Data Types and Typing

This section describes PXL-supported data types and the factors that determine how typing works within PXL.

Variables can be explicitly declared with a type. For example,

```
i : integer = 1 ;  // i is declared as an integer
```

Variables can be implicitly typed based on the return type of the operator. For example,

```
a : double = 1.1203; b : double = 2.0213; c = a + b;            // c is implicitly the type of "double"
```

## Supported Data Types

PXL supports most primitive types and some tool-specific data types.

## Primitive Types

Table 47 shows the primitive data types supported by PXL.

| Data type                                      | Description                                                                                              |
|------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| integer                                        | Integer; size is implementation-defined, generally 32-bit signed values.                                 |
| double                                         | Double-precision floating-point; size is defined at the time of implementation, generally 64-bit values. |
| boolean                                        | True or false                                                                                            |
| string                                         | Sequence of characters; supporting escape sequences to include special characters.                       |
| handle                                         | An opaque data type, used to track data objects external to the PXL program itself.                      |
| constraint of double and constraint of integer | Concise representation of a set of contiguous double values or integer values.                           |
| predicate_handle                               | Boolean expression with special consideration for evaluating layer identifiers as empty or non-empty.    |

Table 47 Primitive Types

<!-- image -->

## integer

Here are examples of integer declarations:

```
i : integer;     // declared but not initialized i : integer = 1; // declared and initialized
```

## string

Defines a string of zero or more characters. The string type is initialized from a string literal. For example,

```
s : string = "xyzzy";
```

The string type supports the operations shown in Table 48 on any expression of string type.

Table 48 String Type Operations

| Operation   | e2 type   | Return   | Modifies e1 Comment   | Modifies e1 Comment                                                                      |
|-------------|-----------|----------|-----------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| e1.empty()  | --        | boolean  | no                    | Returns true if the string is empty, that is the string is "" ; otherwise returns false. |
| e1.size()   | --        | integer  | no                    | Returns the number of characters in the string.                                          |

## handle

An internal representation for an externally managed object. The type handle has a string representation that is unique for each externally managed object.

## constraint of double and constraint of integer

Constraint of double and constraint of integer are mathematical ranges for dimensional rule values. These constraints provide an intuitive mechanism for describing parameters such as DRC spacing distances.

If the type of constraint is unspecified, it implies that the range is a constraint of double.

The constraint data types support the operations shown in Table 49 on an expression of this type.

| Operation       | e2 type   | Return   | Modifies e1 Comment                                                                 |
|-----------------|-----------|----------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| e1.contains(e2) | item      | boolean  | no Returns true if the e2 value is within the range specified by the e1 constraint. |

Table 49 Constraint of Double and Constraint of Integer Operations

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Table 49 Constraint of Double and Constraint of Integer Operations (Continued)

| Operation     | e2 type   | Return          | Modifies e1   | Comment                                                                                                                                           |
|---------------|-----------|-----------------|---------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| e1.category() | --        | enum            | no            | Returns the enumerator of the constraint from the predefined enumeration constraint category. See Table 50.                                       |
| e1.lo()       | --        | integer/dou ble | no            | For binary constraints, returns the lower bound of the constraint: a double for a constraint of double; an integer for a constraint of integer. 3 |
| e1.hi()       | --        | integer/dou ble | no            | For binary constraints, returns the upper bound of the constraint: a double for a constraint of double; an integer for a constraint of integer. 3 |

The constraint data type can only be created by assignment from another like-typed constraint or from a literal constant, as shown in Table 50.

Table 50 Constraint Categories

| Literal   | Description                                             | Constraint category   |
|-----------|---------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------|
| [a,b]     | Closed range from a to b, including both endpoints      | CONSTRAINT_GELE       |
| (a,b)     | Open range from a to b, omitting the endpoints          | CONSTRAINT_GTLT       |
| [a,b)     | Half-open range from a to b, including a but not b      | CONSTRAINT_GELT       |
| (a,b]     | Half-open range from a to b, omitting a but including b | CONSTRAINT_GTLE       |
| >= a      | Range of all numbers greater than or equal to a         | CONSTRAINT_GE         |
| > a       | Range of all numbers greater than a                     | CONSTRAINT_GT         |
| <= a      | Range of all numbers less than or equal to a            | CONSTRAINT_LE         |
| < a       | Range of all numbers less than a                        | CONSTRAINT_LT         |
| == a      | Range containing only the number a                      | CONSTRAINT_EQ         |
| != a      | Range containing all numbers except a                   | CONSTRAINT_NE         |

Both lo() and hi() are valid for all constraints. For single-ended constraints, both functions are defined to return the single endpoint, 'a'. For double-ended constraints, lo() returns 'a' and hi() returns 'b'.

3. For unary constraints, such as == and &gt;, both e1.lo() and e1.hi() return the single limit.

## Examples

Here are some examples.

- Constraint of integer
- Constraint of double
- [2,8] contains all real numbers in the range including 2.0 and 8.0
- (2,8) contains all the real numbers in the range except 2.0 and 8.0
- Declaration example
- Assignment examples

```
[2,8] contains the values 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 (2,8) contains the values 3, 4, 5, 6, 7
```

```
a_value : constraint of double = [2.0,8.0];
```

```
distance <= 2.0          // All values less than or equal to 2.0 distance = <= 2.0        // All values less than or equal to 2.0 distance = [ 2.0, 8.0 )  // All values >= 2.0 and < 8.0 count = 5                // Count is exactly equal to 5 count = ==5              // Count is exactly equal to 5
```

## Note:

The symbols such as == and &lt;= are part of the constraint. The assignment operator = is optional for variables expecting a constraint type. However, if a variable of the constraint type is on the right side, the assignment operator is necessary:

```
my_constraint: constraint of double = < 5.0; external1(layer1, distance = my_constraint ); external1(layer1, distance <5);                // same as above external1(layer1, distance = < 5);             // same as above
```

## predicate\_handle

A Boolean expression enclosed in double brackets[[…]]. Any sort of Boolean logic containing at least one layer name or violation name is allowed. A layer name is special inside the predicate expression because at runtime, it evaluates to true if the layer has data, or false if the layer is empty. Violation objects also evaluate to true if there are violations and false if there are no violations.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

In runset functions, predicate\_handle arguments control the operation of a given function based on the expression evaluation:

- true : The function operates as normal.
- false : The function produces an empty output layer.

## For example:

```
temp_layer = and(poly, diff, predicate = [[metal1]]); If metal1 is empty, the and() function is skipped, and temp_layer is empty.
```

## User-Defined Structures and Types

In addition to the primitive types, PXL supports the structures and types shown in Table 51.

Table 51 User-Defined Types

| User-defined type   | Salient features                                                                                                                          |
|---------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| newtype...          | Defines a type.                                                                                                                           |
| enum of...          | Defines a list of enumerated elements.                                                                                                    |
| list of...          | Defines a list of elements.                                                                                                               |
| hash of...          | Converts a list of elements of one data type to another data type.                                                                        |
| struct of...        | Defines a composite type consisting of multiple variables.                                                                                |
| function            | Defines a user-defined function that can be passed to another user-defined function and can be called as if it were an ordinary variable. |

## newtype...

A newtype declares a type of new variable. It does not define a variable. Each type is unique.

The following example is of a valid type definition:

```
/* * define a new type, direction. */ direction: newtype enum of { up, down, left, right, all // trailing comma is allowed }; /* define two distinct types */ T1: newtype integer;
```

```
T2: newtype integer; /* define objects of the two types */ o1: T1; o2: T2;
```

The following example is of an invalid type definition:

```
/* given the definitions above, o1 and o2 are of * different types, therefore they cannot be compared * and this is an error */ if (o1 == o2) { ... }
```

Here is an example of defining and using a new data type called direction. It has four allowed values.

```
direction : newtype enum of { NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST }; compass : direction;  // Declare compass as type "direction" compass = EAST;       // Assign a legal value to "compass"
```

## enum of...

Defines a set of names (enum literals) distinct from other types. The PXL coding standard is for enum literals to be all uppercase characters.

## For example,

```
t3: newtype enum of { X, Y, Z,               // Trailing comma is not needed; silently discarded. };
```

## Here is another example:

```
direction : newtype enum of { NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST }; compass : direction;         // Declare compass as type "direction" compass = EAST;              // Assign a legal value to "compass"
```

An enum can share names with other enumeration types without error:

```
t1_e : newtype enum of { NONE, TOP, BOTTOM, ALL };
```

<!-- image -->

```
Data Types and Typing t2_e : newtype enum of { NONE, LEFT, RIGHT, ALL };
```

Cross-type operations are not allowed. Also, within one type definition, you cannot use the same name more than one time.

This example shows a cross-type operation. This operation is not legal:

```
v1 : t1_e;    // NONE, TOP, BOTTOM, ALL v1 = NONE;    // Legal assignment v1 = TOP;     // Legal assignment v1 = RIGHT;   // Illegal assignment v2 : t2_e;    // NONE, LEFT, RIGHT, ALL v2 = NONE;    // Legal assignment if (v2 == v1) // Illegal
```

## list of...

Lists are arrays of objects.

- All of the objects are of the same type. This type is allowed to be empty or to contain duplicate objects.
- It can be processed using the foreach() looping construct.
- Lists can be addressed by an index number using brackets ([ ]).

See Nested Containers on page 228' for information about a list of lists.

This type supports the operations shown in Table 52.

| Operation       | e2 type   | Return   | Modifies e1   | Comment                                                                 |
|-----------------|-----------|----------|---------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| e1.empty()      | --        | boolean  | no            | Returns true if the list contains no elements; otherwise returns false. |
| e1.size()       | --        | integer  | no            | Returns the number of elements in the list.                             |
| e1.contains(e2) | item      | boolean  | no            | Returns true if e2 is an element of the e1 list.                        |
| e1.front()      | --        | item     | no            | Returns a copy of the first element of the list.                        |
| e1.back()       | --        | item     | no            | Returns a copy of the last element of the list.                         |

Table 52 List Operations

<!-- image -->

Table 52 List Operations (Continued)

| Operation         | e2 type   | Return   | Modifies e1   | Comment                                                                                 |
|-------------------|-----------|----------|---------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| e1.chop_back()    | --        | list     | no            | Returns a copy of the e1 list with the last element removed.                            |
| e1.chop_front()   | --        | list     | no            | Returns a copy of the e1 list with the first element removed.                           |
| e1.append(e2)     | item      | list     | no            | Returns a copy of the e1 list with e2 added to the back of the list.                    |
| e1.prepend(e2)    | item      | list     | no            | Returns a copy of the e1 list with e2 added to the front of the list.                   |
| e1.push_front(e2) | item      | void     | yes           | Adds a copy of the e2 expression to the front of the list.                              |
| e1.push_back(e2)  | item      | void     | yes           | Adds a copy of the e2 expression to the back of the list.                               |
| e1.pop_front()    | --        | void     | yes           | Removes the first element of the list.                                                  |
| e1.pop_back()     | --        | void     | yes           | Removes the last element of the list.                                                   |
| e1.merge(e2)      | list      | list     | no            | con ate i l s , Returns a copy of the e1 list with the e2 list concatenated to the end. |
| e1.remove(e2)     | item      | void     | yes           | Removes all values in the e1 list that are equal to the e2 expression.                  |

## The following are examples of legal code:

```
x: layer = ... ; MyPartition: list of layer = PartitionLayer(L1); foreach (part in MyPartition) { ... } if (MyPartition.contains(x)) { ... } i : integer = MyPartition.size(); The following example shows how to concatenate a list: list1 : list of integer = { 1, 2, 3 }; list2 : list of integer = { 10, 20, 30 }; list3 : list of integer = list1.merge(list2); list3 now has the value { 1, 2, 3, 10, 20, 30 };
```

<!-- image -->

## Here is an example of initializing and using a list of strings.

```
// declare myList to be a list of strings, uninitialized myList : list of string; // declare myList to be a list of strings, initialized myList : list of string = { "this", "is" , "a", "list" }; // myList[0] = "this" // myList[3] = "list"
```

## Built-in list operator functions are supported. For example,

```
myList : list of string = { "this", "is" , "a", "list" }; s = myList.size();         // returns the size of a list: s is "4" a = myList.front();        // a contains a copy of L1[0]: a is "this" myList.pop_front();        // removes the first element of the list, // the list is now { "is", "a", "list" } myList.pop_back();         // removes the last element of the list, // the list is now { "is", "a" } myList.push_front("xyz");  // adds a new element containing "xyz" // to the front of the list. // the list is now { "xyz", "is", "a" } myList.push_back("bar");   // adds a new element containing "bar" // to the back of the list. // the list is now { "xyz", "is", "a", "bar" }
```

## hash of...

Defines a mapping from one data type to another. The source type is called the key type; the destination type is called the value type. That is, the hash defines an array of key/value pairs.

This type requires that the key type be string, integer, or enum, or a type derived from one of these three types. It cannot be a double. The value type can be of any previously defined type.

The following example creates a hash that converts integers to strings. In this case, the key type is integer and the value type is string. This type is initialized using the =&gt; operator.

```
t1_h : newtype hash of integer to string; t2_h : newtype hash of string to integer; h1 : t1_h = { 1  => "a", 2  => "b", 26 => "z" }; h2 : t2_h = { "xyzzy" => 1,
```

<!-- image -->

```
"plugh" => 10, "help"  => 100 };
```

## Here is an example of how a derived type can be used:

```
t1 : newtype integer; h1_h : newtype hash of t1 to string; x : h1_h = { 1 => "a" } ;
```

The hash of... type can be assigned element-wise using subscripts:

```
x = h1[203]; h1[30] = "ad";
```

The hash of... type supports the member operations shown in Table 53.

Table 53 Hash Operations

| Operation             | e2 type               | Return             | Modifies e1   | Comment                                                                                                                                                           |
|-----------------------|-----------------------|--------------------|---------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| e1.contains_key(e2)   | key type of hash      |                    | no            | Returns true if e2 is a key to the e1 hash table. Effectively the same as e1.keys().contains(e2) but with possibly better runtime performance.                    |
| e1.contains_value(e2) | value type of hash    |                    | no            | Returns true if e2 is a value for some entry in the e1 hash table. Effectively the same as e1.values().contains(e2) but with possibly better runtime performance. |
| e1.empty()            | --                    | boolean            | no            | Returns true if the hash contains no elements; otherwise returns false.                                                                                           |
| e1.keys()             | --                    | list of key type   | no            | Returns a list of all key values; the list does not have duplicate values.                                                                                        |
| e1.size()             | --                    | integer            | no            | Returns the number of elements in the hash.                                                                                                                       |
| e1.values()           | --                    | list of value type | no            | Returns a list of all values; the list can contain duplicates, based on the content of the hash.                                                                  |
| e1.merge(e2)          | hash matching e1 type | hash               | no            | Returns a copy of the e1 hash with the keys and values of e2 concatenated to the end; any key that exists in e1 and e2 takes its                                  |

value from e2.

<!-- image -->

## Table 53 Hash Operations (Continued)

| Operation     | e2 type   | Return   | Modifies e1 Comment                                                                       |
|---------------|-----------|----------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| e1.remove(e2) | item      | void     | yes Removes the e2 key from the e1 hash. There is no effect if the e2 key does not exist. |

## Here is another example:

```
alpha_h : newtype hash of string to integer; alpha : alpha_h = {       // declare and initialize key => value pairs "a" => 1, "b" => 2, "c" => 3 }; y = alpha["b"];          // The value of y is "2" keyList = alpha.keys();  // A list of the keys in alpha
```

## struct of...

Defines a distinct type identified by the user-supplied name. It must have at least one member and member names must be unique. The members can be of different types.

Here is an example structure that defines a point by its geometric coordinates:

```
point: newtype struct of { x: integer; y: integer; };
```

The struct of... type can contain initial values that are used as defaults for structure creation.

```
t3_s : newtype struct of { x: integer; y: integer = 76;   // initializer z: string = "hi";  // initializer }; t4_s : newtype struct of { a: integer = 106;  // initializer b: string = "boo"; // initializer };
```

The struct of... type can be assigned from a C-style initializer or from a list of namevalue pairs. The following example shows assignment using the types defined in the previous example.

```
s3 : t3_s = { 10, z = "bye" };  // note that 'y' defaults // to the value 76 // the defaults cause s4 to have a=106, b="boo" s4 : t4_s = { };
```

<!-- image -->

Here is another example.

```
shoebox : newtype struct of { style : string = "Tennis Shoe"; shoe_size : double = 10.5; }; box : shoebox; shoe = box.style;          // shoe is "Tennis shoe", the default box.style = "Dress Shoe";  // Reassign the member box.style // create a new shoebox with a different kind of shoe box2 : shoebox = {"Boat Shoe", 9};
```

## function

Allows a function to be passed to another user function. The function that is passed can be used as though it were a global function. For example,

```
// input file #include <icv.rh> xyzzy : function (void) returning void { note("abcd"); } plugh : function ( f : function(void) returning void ) returning void { f(); } plugh(xyzzy);  // summary file shows "abcd" in output when plugh runs
```

## Nested Types

Types can be combined to form nested types, such as

- list of struct
- list of enum

For example, using the shoebox struct definition in the example in struct of... on page 224:

```
box : list of shoebox = { { "Walking", 12 }, { "High Heel", 7 } }; A = box[0].style;           // A is "Walking" B = box[1].shoe_size;       // B is 7
```

## Type Analysis

This section describes how PXL handles data types in special cases, such as when one data type is passed in an argument but another data type is expected.

In cases where PXL encounters one data type when another data type is expected, PXL performs automatic type conversion whenever appropriate. The rules that are used to perform automatic type conversion are discussed in the following sections.

<!-- image -->

## Standard Arithmetic Conversions

When there is a mismatch between the arithmetic type demanded by an expression and the arithmetic type found, conversions are done as shown in Table 54.

Table 54 Arithmetic Conversions

| While expecting ...   | Allow integer   | Allow constraint of integer   | Allow double   | Allow constraint of double   |
|-----------------------|-----------------|-------------------------------|----------------|------------------------------|
| integer               | Yes 4           | No 5                          | No             | No                           |
| constraint of integer | Yes             | Yes                           | No             | No                           |
| double                | Yes             | No                            | Yes            | No                           |
| constraint of double  | Yes             | Yes                           | Yes            | Yes                          |

These conversions are only applied when required by the types of the expression. In particular, integer-typed expressions are not converted to double unless required by the context.

When converting an integer or double to a constraint, the resultant constraint appears as if it had been written using the == unary constraint (CONSTRAINT\_EQ).

```
f: function ( c: constraint ) returning void { ... } f( (1.0, 26.0) );       // constraint is ok f( 2.0 );               // single value is ok also f( 42 );                // single integer is accepted
```

## Comparing Doubles

Because the type double is an approximation of the real numbers, there are occasionally accumulated errors that cause apparently equivalent operations to produce different results. PXL has special functions for comparing doubles while accounting for such small errors. These special functions are described in the Equivalence Comparison Functions and Double Comparison Functions of the Math Functions section in the 'Utility Functions' chapter of the IC Validator Reference Manual .

## Note:

A warning is reported whenever there is a direct comparison (either == or !=) involving one of the double-related types.

4. Yes indicates that the conversion is allowed.
5. No indicates that the conversion is not allowed. The operation resulted in an error.

<!-- image -->

## Type Promotion

When a list is expected and an expression of the same type as that contained by the list is found, the expression is promoted from a single item to a list containing that item.

## Parameter Passing

Function parameters that are qualified with either output or input-output must have matching argument values. The rules previously described do not apply. For example, when a function expects a constraint argument that is marked as out, providing the name of an integer-typed variable is not legal because the conversion that is required is not legal.

## String Concatenation

Any expression of the types shown in Table 55 can be appended to a string expression using the standard addition operator (+).

Table 55 String Concatenation

| Type                  | Resultant string appended                                             |
|-----------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| integer               | Value of the integer expression                                       |
| double                | Value of the double expression                                        |
| handle                | Textual representation of the handle; unique for each distinct object |
| string                | Content of the string                                                 |
| boolean               | Either true or false                                                  |
| constraint of integer | Equivalent constraint literal expression                              |
| constraint of double  | Equivalent constraint literal expression                              |
| user-defined enum     | Name of the enum literal represented by the expression                |

When you are working with strings, remember

- When the left side of an addition operator (+) is a string, the result is a string.
- The addition operator (+) is not symmetric for string-valued expressions: a + b != b + a
- There are no spaces added between subsequent items appended to a string, so you might see unexpected results, such as in the following examples:

```
s : string; s = "hello " + 10 + " " + (1 == 0); // s now contains the string "hello 10 false"
```

<!-- image -->

```
c : constraint = ( 10, 40 ]; s = "" + c; // s now contains the string "(10.,40.]", because the // type of "c" is constraint of double mye : newtype enum of { A, B, C, D, X }; t : mye = X; s = "" + t + A + B; // s now contains the string "XAB" s = "" + 11 + 3.14 + (1 == 1); // s now contains the string "113.14true" s = "" + (11 + 3.14) + (1 == 1); // s now contains the string "14.14true"
```

## Default Injection

When processing a function call, parameters for which no value is given assume the defaults, if any, from the function prototype. A parameter with no default or specified value results in an error.

Similarly, when processing a literal structure, members for which no value is given assume the defaults, if any, from the newtype structure definition. A member with no default or specified value results in an error.
